As you know, I am very vehement in my disapproval of the death penalty.
I think it is inhumane, and disgusting.
So here is an exposé on American executions.
What follows is not a neutral accounting of options but a taxonomy of state-sanctioned violence, each method a different architecture of the same cruelty.
I want you to sit with the details, not skim past them.
These are not abstractions — they are things done to human bodies, in your name, by your government.
1) Firing Squad – In Idaho and Oklahoma, the firing squad is an option.
In Oklahoma, this method is authorized only if a current method is found unconstitutional.
The inmate is typically restrained in a chair, a target placed over the heart, while a team of marksmen takes aim at a living person.
Utah also offers this method, but only for inmates who chose this option before it was eliminated.
All three states offer lethal injection as an option.
If the members of the firing squad have good aim, death comes fairly quickly from blood loss.
Sandbags are placed all around the inmate to soak up the blood.
2) Hanging – New Hampshire and Washington offer this as a way to execute an inmate.

The word 'hanging' carries a kind of frontier plainness that obscures what it actually describes: a body dropped, a rope pulled taut, a neck asked to bear the full consequence of the state's judgment.
New Hampshire only authorizes hanging if lethal injection cannot be used.
Washington gives the inmate the choice between hanging and lethal injection.
The prisoner would be weighed prior to the hanging to attempt to avoid a botched execution.
If the rope length is incorrect, the inmate could be decapitated, or fracture-dislocation is not rapid.
Other reasons for fracture-dislocation to not occur would be strong neck muscles, an unusually light weighing prisoner, or the noose not being positioned properly.
When fracture-dislocation does not happen, the inmate dies from slow asphyxiation, which can take up to 45 minutes.
3) Gas Chamber – Arizona, California, Maryland, Missouri, and Wyoming use this method.
Wyoming will only use it if lethal injection is found unconstitutional.
People sentenced to death in Arizona before 11/15/92 can choose between lethal injection and the gas chamber.
California gives the inmate choice between lethal injection and the gas chamber.
Maryland gives the inmate the choice between lethal injection and the gas chamber as long as they were condemned to die before 3/25/94.
Missouri statute leaves it unclear just who chooses the option – the inmate or the Missouri Department of Corrections.

The word 'chamber' suggests something sterile and architectural, a contained and managed space, but what happens inside it is neither sterile nor managed — the condemned person breathes in cyanide gas and their body fights back with everything it has.
They are aware and in agony for most if not the entire time.
The eyes burn, the throat seizes, and the body convulses as it refuses, involuntarily and uselessly, to accept what is being done to it.
Death comes from hypoxia (the cutting off of oxygen to the brain).
4) Electrocution – Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Illinois, Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia use this method.
Oklahoma authorizes electrocution only if lethal injection is found unconstitutional, and Illinois only if lethal injection is found unconstitutional or cannot be given.

Each jolt that fails to kill is not a procedural retry — it is a distinct event, a second or third violence visited upon a person who may still be conscious, still feeling, still present inside the body being destroyed.
Alabama, Florida, South Carolina, and Virginia let the prisoner choose this method or lethal injection.
Arkansas lets inmates choose (if convicted before 7/4/83).
All others must use lethal injection.
Prisoners in Kentucky convicted before March 31, 1998 can choose lethal injection or electrocution.
All others must take lethal injection.
In Tennessee, inmates convicted after 1/1/99 must use lethal injection, those prior may choose electrocution.
In electrocution, it sometimes takes more than one jolt to kill the condemned.
Sometimes their eyeballs will pop out and rest on their cheeks, and in some cases they have caught on fire.
5)Lethal Injection – 36 states, plus the US military and the US government use this as either the sole method of execution or as an alternative.

The states not already mentioned as using this method are: Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Montana, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, and Texas.
With lethal injection, death results from anesthetic overdose and respiratory and cardiac arrest while the condemned person is unconscious.
The clinical tidiness of that description is precisely the problem — it implies a mercy that the chemistry does not always deliver.
The chemical pancuronioum bromide, which is widely used for lethal injections, could leave the prisoner wide awake and unable to speak or cry out as they slowly suffocate.
The drug paralyzes skeletal muscles, but does not effect the brain or nerves.
In fact, the American Veterinary Medical Association condemns the use of that drug in putting down animals “because the animal may perceive pain and distress after it is immobilized”.
Now what do you think about executions?
We went to Westchester Union Square Hospital today, which is near Tremont Street in the Bronx, to visit the almighty sexiness that is my greatgrandmother.
She looked good - the nurse says she has a gallstone and that the doctor would talk with her tommorrow about removing her gallbladder.
:-/ I dont know... surgery is very dangerous with 90 year old women because of the effect that anestesia has on their body -- it has the potential to kill her.
The thought of it sat in my chest the whole time we were there, quiet and heavy, the way certain things do when you know you are not supposed to say them out loud.
Even though she is getting medicine from the IV, she is doing well, and is rather perky.
She fussed over the card we gave her - 'No soy negrita!'
The woman on the card is fucking tanned, take.
She would joke around with me, 'Eres feo.'
Then she would laugh.
'A quien do you belong to?'
I would point to her and say, 'You.'
and she would giggle in her old woman cackle.
My cousin Iris was there too, sitting close to the bed with her hand near abuela's arm, the way you sit next to someone when you already know how to be in their silences.
Iris and abuela are really close (live in the same apartment building), related as aunt-and-niece.
You could see it in the way abuela reached for her without looking, the way you reach for something you know will always be there.
Only 30% of her lung mass is usable - she will die soon.
But boy-oh-boy, you have not lived until you see someone with emphasemia laugh.
It comes out ragged and enormous, this big rattling thing that her whole small body has to work for, and somehow it is the funniest and most heartbreaking sound you have ever heard in your life.
And she laughed like that at her own jokes, at my face, at the card, at everything, Dios mio, at everything.
I said goodbye to abuela, considering this may be the last time I ever see her alive.
Afterall, Andy Warhol died from complications of gallbladder surgery.
*cringes* And for the second half of our visit, I swapped places with my dad, to watch Jenna.
We sat in the small eatery next to the first floor waiting room.
Jenna got a thing with corn in it and seemed perfectly satisfied, which, fine, good for her.
Corn does not equal cheese in my world.
Dios me bendiga , I guess I'm  chocha like that.
I played I-Spy with Jenna.
I told her to look for something red, in a room were 95% of the things were horrifyingly red and pink.
When she couldn't guess, I told her she lost, and tried to read more of Hemingway's The Old Man & The Sea, then stopped because I wanted to kill myself.
Hemingway's stories = Nesdill story.
We drove Iris home from the hospital.

She was quiet most of the way, looking out the window at the Bronx moving past her, and I did not ask her what she was thinking because I already knew, more or less, or at least I knew the shape of it.
In the end she was okay, and I listened to Celine Dion on the ride back home.
We stopped at Burger King, and I wound up eating french fries for dinner.
It felt like the right thing to eat after a day like this — something hot and bad for you and immediate, something that asks nothing of you.
The fries were so damn salty, I worry that my body will now retain water, and my feet will swell up.
Today did give me alot to think about though.
Reexamination of life, its values, its mysteries, its horrors, and so on.
I keep thinking that if she goes, the funeral will probably fall on some inconvenient week, the kind where you already had plans, and that is a terrible thing to think but it is also just true.
But then again, I guess there really is no  good  time for a funeral.
Staring at her lifeless body would scare me though.
I learn to hold onto what I have, and be grateful.
Because one day, I may turn out just like the sexiness that is la chula de bronx - my greatgrandmother.
Life is a bitch.
Just so happens that some bitches.... are nice.

The situation in Sudan and the surrounding Darfur region makes me want to vomit.
It is horrific and disgusting.
What is more disgusting is the fact that the international governments are doing nothing.
Kofi Annan is begging, and the United States does what?
They issued a statement.
That didn't do...well...anything!
We can go into Iraq to 'liberate their people' and take their oil, but god-forbid, when an actual humanitarian crisis emerges, we do anything to help.
The desert villages of Darfur have been emptied and torched, and the world watched it happen the way you watch weather on television — from somewhere safe, with the sound low.
Rascism between the blacks, and arabs was caused by some economic problems in the 1970s.
The actions of the Janjaweed has affected more the 1 million people, and is called the greatest humanitarian crisis to hit Africa.
The UN calls it 'borderline-genocide'.
And yet the international community is doing... the US is doing.... you guessed it - pretty much, nothing.
The international community calls it a crisis.
A crisis is a broken pipe.
This is something else.

A child in Darfur carries everything she owns in a plastic bag, and the government of Sudan — the same government that armed the men who burned her home — sits in Khartoum, untouched, while the world debates the precise vocabulary of atrocity.
As if the effect of AIDS wasn't bad enough for the region.
I think the most atrocious thing these Janjaweed members are doing, is raping the women and female children.
The family values in Sudan state that rape is unforgiveable.
And the victims of rape are ostricized by their family, husbands, and friends.
As if it was their fault that they were raped!
The United States refuses to give more money to the UN AIDS fund, and will not forget the billions of dollars of debt the african countries find themselves to be in, but cant afford to repay.
But today, I read in the google news that the government of Sudan sentenced 10 members of the janjaweed to amputation of their limbs, and life in jail.
Somehow, despite all of the torture they have done, and all of the lives they have taken, feel that they are victims of their government.
The government hired them to do this.
The government, in addition to these men, need to pay.
And why do they need to lose their limbs?

The crime was not in their hands — the crime was in the orders they followed, the state that paid them, the system that made them a weapon and then called them criminals when the world finally looked.
I am not happy yet.
Justice without accountability is just punishment theater, and ten pairs of hands means nothing while the men who gave the orders keep their offices, their borders, their silence.
An international court needs to step in, and take action.
A new government is needed to watch over the country of Sudan, and the biggest economies in the world need to help out a bit.
Let's stop building new sports stadiums, and start helping people who need it most.

We know you are morphing your body so you can look more like Peter Pan, the nose totally gives you away on that one.
At this point the CDC should have a form for classifying Michael Jackson's race, sex, and species — just a standard government checkbox that reads 'OTHER: see attached.'
Do we need an anthropologist to come in and study your bone structure?
Oooohhh, riiiight, you didn't touch that boy... you only had sleepovers where you slept in the same bed!

Martha Stewart, the queen of perfection, and home accessories, lied to the government about how she sold Imclone.
Oh my goodness, she LIED!
When she lies, we send her to jail for 5 monthes.
For a stock sale.
Let that sink in.
A woman who taught America how to fold napkins is now behind bars, and somehow that feels like justice to people.
Jail is supposed to be a place we send people who are a threat to society.
Martha Stewart is a threat to no one — not to your safety, not to your savings, not to anything except the uncomfortable idea that wealthy women shouldn't get to protect their own money.
And why are we spending tax payers' money to keep in her jail?
It's a waste of money.
If anyone of us found ourselves in the same position she did, we would have done the same thing - sell our shares in order to save our money.
Don't deny it - you love money, and we all have friends in benefitial places.
Martha was trying to live the American dream, with her money, her success, and her line of products.
And now she has found herself a prisoner of politics and the hate of the public.
People LOVE to HATE her.
She was too perfect.
Too put-together.
Too successful for someone the public had already decided wasn't allowed to be.
She made aspiration look effortless, and when she stumbled, everyone who ever felt judged by a perfectly set table got to feel something ugly and satisfying.
Clinton lied to us about his extramartial affair with Monica Lewinsky, and he was impeached.
But he finished his term.
He kept his career.
He kept his reputation, and half the country still cheers for him at every appearance.
Bush is a murderer, something that is far worse than anything Clinton or Stewart ever did, and he gets no consequences!
But after Martha was sentenced, she compared her jailtime to that of Nelson Mandela's.
Mandela was thrown in a South African jail, and beaten everyday for 26 years for conspiring to overthrow the discriminatory Apartheid.
Martha is going to jail for lying to the US government about her dealings with her shares of Imclone, and is being sentenced to 5 monthes in a waspy jail.
I can totally see the connection, Martha!
*rolls eyes* Look hun, I disagree with the reason you are going to jail, but do not push my limits.
Your case has no connection to that of Nelson Mandela - unless your Kmart line is suppoed to liberate the people of a hateful regime.

Just an annual checkup; so i woke up at 11 am for my 12:30 appointment.
Everything went well: I arrived and signed in, and waited awhile until they gave me the little cup to pee in.
And I just stared at it, thinking, 'SHIT!
I don't hafta go right now!
This is alot of pressure to put on one person!'
But I walked to the bathroom to try anyways.
They strategically place the restroom on the other side of the waiting room, so you got to walk that long stretch, and people are looking at you, and then at the cup, and sneering.
Like, 'Eww, you have to pee in that.'
Nothing like a roomful of strangers watching you do the cup walk of shame past the magazine rack and the sad little fish tank.

Then I called my friends, because what else do you do after a doctor's appointment — go home and think about your vertebrae?

We drove down in two minivans, somebody's dad got a speeding ticket in Virginia, and we all thought that was the funniest thing that had ever happened to anyone — and looking back, I think it was the last time I felt completely, uncomplicatedly myself around them.
Now they are moving to North Carolina, and it all seems so sad.
Then I realized, I don't know them anymore.
I dont KNOW them - who they are, what makes them smile, and what makes them laugh.
On the ride up, I blasted Madonna in my ears, as I thought that over; that I would be saying goodbye to people I didn't really know today.
Suddenly, as we walked to the restaruent on Mott Street, I realized: I know them, but it is them who don't know me.
My sexuality pretty much defines me.
And for people who don't know about it, I put some kind of shell in front of me.
I never showed them the real me, and I never came out to them.
In fear of how they would react, or losing these friends forever, I shut them out.

There was a moment at Myrtle Beach, maybe three years back, when Gracie asked me why I never talked about girls, and I laughed it off and said something about being focused on school, and she accepted that, and I watched the real answer sink somewhere inside me like a stone dropped in deep water — and I had been listening to it fall ever since.
Dinner proved to be something I hadn't expected.
When I think of HopKee, I think of: dirty Korean waiters, who need to learn how to use deoderant, dirty utensils, cramped and underground hideout, disgusting food, and people who I feel awkward with.
I wasn't expecting to have fun, but I did.
The food was good: ungchoy, chow fung, and white rice.
Hearty Korean cuisine.

Then Angé said something about the Myrtle Beach trip — the wrong name, the wrong year, completely misremembering the whole thing — and everyone corrected her at once, loudly and over each other, and the table erupted, and for a second it was just noise and laughter and nobody was moving anywhere.
I guess I was wrong; we both knew eachother, what makes us laugh, and smile.
We discussed the memories we had of Myrtle Beach, and of all of our inside jokes over the years.
15 years of inside jokes, and memories, all summarized and compressed in a few hours.
It was quite the farewell.
When we left HopKee, we walked the damp streets of Chinatown.
Rain was still washing away the worries of everyone on the street - and we walked over to Little Italy.
The streets were closed for a rained-out festival, and the hard rain calmed to a smooth drizzle.
We stopped at Ferrara's, an amazing Italian bakery, and I had two scoops of pistachio ice cream, and a fork-full of Gracie's tiramisu.
It all went down my throat smoothly.
Then we hit the streets of Little Italy and Chinatown.

The cobblestones were slick and dark, the festival tents empty and dripping, vendor tables bare under plastic sheeting — the whole neighborhood feeling like it had been set up for something that never quite arrived, and the six of us moving through it slowly, nobody rushing, the drizzle settling on our shoulders, Chinatown's fish-market smell giving way to the faint sweetness of cannoli from somewhere we couldn't see, and the streets conspiring, it felt like, to make every step toward that corner take a little longer than it should.
On the corner of Worth and Mott Street, the darkness etching shadows on our chiseled faces, and rain mixing in with tears, we said goodbye.

Gracie pulled me into a hug that lasted long enough that neither of us had to say anything, and when she let go she just looked at me once, and nodded, like she knew something she hadn't known at dinner, or maybe had always known and was only now letting me see that she did.
But deep within our hearts, we know that distance cannot seperate the souls of the CW Post Clan.

Ahh this was such a good paper :)                        President Bill Clinton             What comes to mind when you hear the name Bill Clinton?
Usually the 1998 scandal involving Monica Lewinsky.

But the name also belongs to the longest peacetime economic expansion in American history, to a budget surplus that had not existed since the Johnson administration, and to a president who left office with the highest end-of-term approval rating in modern history.
Before he ever entered the White House, Clinton had already built a record that most politicians spend entire careers reaching for.
He was a governor who lost his office, then won it back — a detail that says something about the kind of persistence that would later define his presidency.
His path to Washington was not inherited or assumed, but earned through years of working inside the political machinery of one of the country's smaller, poorer states.
Clinton graduated from Georgetown University, and in 1968 won a Rhodes Scholarship to Oxford University.
He then received his law degree in 1973 from Yale University, and entered politics in Arkansas.
In 1976, Clinton was elected Arkansas Attorney General, and then won the governor’s race in 1978.
After losing the election for a second term, he then regained the office 4 years later, and served until he defeated George Bush and Ross Perot in the 1992 presidential election.
During Clinton’s first year in office, he focused on passing legislation that improves health care and family life.
He signed the Family and Medical Leave Act in 1993, which allowed millions of working parents to take unpaid leave for the birth of a child or a family illness without losing their jobs.
That same year, he passed the Brady Bill, which required background checks for handgun purchases and closed a gap in federal law that had existed for decades.
He also signed the largest deficit reduction plan in American history, cutting the federal deficit by $500 billion over five years without raising taxes on the middle class.
Then in 1995, a major Bosnian peace settlement was worked out in Dayton, Ohio, which brought to end the largest campaign of force in the history of NATO’s existence.

That agreement ended a war that had killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions more across the former Yugoslavia, and it was brokered in large part through Clinton's direct diplomatic engagement.
The settlement required Clinton to commit American troops to a peacekeeping mission at a moment when public appetite for foreign intervention was low, a political risk he accepted anyway.
In 1997, the Clinton administration signed the Balanced Act, which eliminates the $290 billion budget deficit by 2002.

Also in 1997, legislation is passed to provide additional children’s education and health care funds, and for the first time in 35 years, a president sighs a bill that modernizes the Food and Drug Administration process.
Then in 1998, for the first time since 1969, the federal government has a budget surplus.
A family that had relied on the Children's Health Insurance Program — created under Clinton in 1997 — could now access coverage that simply had not existed for them the year before.

The surplus itself meant that the federal government was no longer borrowing against the future to pay its current bills, a shift with consequences that reached into every household that carried federal debt indirectly.
These were not abstract numbers on a ledger but changes that moved through the actual structure of daily American life.
Also, the Work Incentives bill was passed, which was one of the most important legislative advances for people with disabilities.

It allowed people with disabilities to return to work without immediately losing their Medicare or Medicaid coverage, removing a barrier that had kept many out of the workforce not by choice but by the cruel arithmetic of the existing system.

Clinton also expanded the Earned Income Tax Credit, which lifted millions of working families out of poverty and put more money directly into the hands of people who spent it in their local economies.
He signed the Violence Against Women Act, which for the first time created federal resources specifically dedicated to prosecuting domestic violence and supporting survivors.

The 1990s were a decade shaped by post-Cold War optimism, a technology boom that was rewriting the economy in real time, and a culture war that was growing louder even as the material conditions of most Americans were improving.
Into that atmosphere came a new kind of political media, one built not on reporting but on opposition, and Rush Limbaugh became its most prominent voice.
Also during Clinton’s presidency, Rush Limbaugh made his radio talk show popular by putting Clinton down, which later, other copy cats followed.
But it didn’t work up to their advantage.
Clinton's approval ratings remained high throughout the attacks, and the prosperity of the era made the criticism difficult to sustain.
The economy added more than 22 million jobs during Clinton's two terms, the most of any presidential administration on record, and unemployment fell to its lowest level in thirty years.
When the attacks were loudest, the stock market was rising and the budget was moving toward balance — the noise and the reality were running in opposite directions.
The cultural pressure of partisan radio was real, but it could not rewrite what people were experiencing in their own lives.
What Limbaugh and his imitators were building was a media infrastructure designed to outlast the prosperity that made their arguments so hard to land in the moment.
The record, in the end, was not written on the radio but in the legislation, the treaties, the budget numbers, and the lives they quietly changed.
In conclusion, during the administration of William Jefferson Clinton, the U.S. enjoyed more peace and economic well being that at any other time in history.
He was the first democratic president to serve a second term since Franklin D. Roosevelt.
He presided over the longest peacetime economic expansion in American history, and left office with a federal budget in surplus for the first time in a generation.
The country he handed to his successor was, by most measurable standards, in better shape than the one he had inherited.
Finally, as a plan to celebrate the millennium in 2000, Clinton called for a great national motivation to end racial discrimination.
This is why I believe Bill Clinton is a true world leader.

Baudrillard talks of the 'procession of simulacra,' and our daily home page or a cursory glance at online sources reveals just such a procession.
The difference between cnn.com, yahoo.com, and I-made-this-up-and-you-believe-it.com seems to be merely a function of repetition and belief in credibility.

Like frames in a Warhol silkscreen, we look with similar aesthetic contentment on endless takes of the same constructed reality, created entirely with the amusement of the audience in mind rather than the accuracy of a given situation.

Like Israel Goldkiss' father in  The Million Dollar Hotel , we must acknowledge that each day, news media in 60 countries decide what 'the Truth' is, and in each one it's different, as it is narrowly tailored to suit the entertainment, consumerism, and ideological needs of its intended audience.
Where, oh where, is Chechnya in my nightly digest?
Our fickle consumer media are selling us sadness in the worst sense: localized regional media promote the isolation of individual cultures from the broad perspective of 'humanity.'

What fills the space left by that missing broad perspective is not silence but noise — the homepage refreshed out of habit, the television left on in the next room, its blue light flickering against the wall like a hearth no one is warming themselves at.
The endless repetition of ideas that are miscontextualized or without original reference.
Like the self-righteous author who writes to see words on a page, we watch to have referential fodder with which we make bland political references in specialized social contexts.
We are a globe obsessed with 'being told' but wholly disinterested in 'finding out.'
We nod at the headline without clicking the link, drop the name of a distant conflict into dinner conversation without being able to find it on a map, and call this being informed.
The distinction has quietly collapsed, and we have been too comfortable in the collapse to notice.

Perhaps not surprisingly, I have to disagree with you.
There is no doubt in my mind that the UN is good for mankind.
The trouble comes from mixing together several different issues, I think.
The question of whether the UN is a good idea is separate from whether the UN, as it currently stands, is functioning well.
These are not the same question, and conflating them is how the argument gets lost before it starts.
I think that some of the basic setup of the organization is flawed.
This isn't news to anyone, not even the members of the United Nations.
The system of permanent veto power is flawed, although I would be hard pressed to come up with a system that isn't.
The funding of the UN is deplorable.
The fact that member nations can simply decline to pay, and face no meaningful consequence for doing so, is not a structural quirk — it is a structural failure.
But much of this can be changed.
Kofi Annan, the secretary general,  urlLink has called for a reanalysis of the UN .
I think that in the wake of the Iraq war, this is absolutely necessary.

Whether or not one agrees with the decision of the Coalition of the Willing to invade Iraq, all evidence seems to indicate that the UN and the security council shot itself in the foot in the events leading up to war.
How can they possibly pass a strongly-worded (at least, for the UN) resolution like  urlLink this one  condemning Iraq for numerous violations and then back it up with nothing?

Although I personally believe that the inspectors should have been given more time in Iraq--and I think that the fact that the US teams are now asking for more time to find the same WMDs confirms that--I still think that the UN had painted itself into a corner in this matter.
So the UN is flawed, no doubt about it.
And, more importantly,  how can it be fixed ?
By excluding people?
By eliminating the representatives of despots?
That is a genuinely hard question, and I won't pretend the answer comes easily.
However, one thing is clear to me: that is  not  the solution to making the UN something useful.

Removing the chairs of bad governments does not remove the governments, and it does not remove the people who live under them — it simply removes them from the table where their fate might otherwise be discussed.

The organization can not function when its most dominant players do not pay their dues, when they practice short-sighted partisan politics, and when they are dishonest about their goals and objectives.
I'm sure that you will respond that this is giving yet another free slice of the pie to undeserving countries--I can hear it now.
I have several different problems with this: first of all, I think that perhaps we have fundamentally different definitions of 'deserving'.
Secondly, I think that the US is just as guilty of wanting hypocrisy as any other country.
The tell is not in any single policy decision but in the quiet assumption that our double standards are principled and everyone else's are merely convenient.
I am proud to be American.
I am happy that, currently, our country is on top of the world, that we are the standard by which every other judges themselves.
I do not think that this position is unearned, or that being on top is an undesirable or even immoral position, as some people seem to.
I have never and will never intentionally critique the US because it is on top.
Still, at the same time, I do not want my country to be the police force for the world.
There are countries whose core values differ sharply from ours, and I think that is not only inevitable but, in many cases, legitimate.
Different histories produce different conclusions, and I find that more interesting than threatening.
I enjoy diversity enough to welcome these disagreements.
And even when there are violations of these core values so atrocious as to merit police action, I would rather that that action not be unilateral.
A world in which that burden is genuinely shared is not a world in which American power disappears — it is a world in which American power is no longer spent on resentment.
Imagine if the US did not have to focus a huge portion of it attention and budget on minding what we view to be the problems of the rest of the world?
Imagine if we did not have to deal with the anger and hatred that will always be associated with such interventions?
Wouldn't that be better for everyone?
The US and the other superpowers--especially the veto powers--are key to making that vision a reality.
We can have philosophical discussion about the demands of the smaller countries, but fundamentally it the actions of a small handful of nations that will determine the longterm efficiency of the UN.
If we choose our actions wisely, perhaps we have a chance to differentiate our time from the 2600 years of human history that precede it.
As anyone who drives can tell you by the thinning of their wallet, the high oil prices of late are still hitting hard.

You notice it most at the pump — that moment when the numbers on the display keep climbing past what you budgeted, past what you paid last month, past what feels reasonable, and you're still only at half a tank.
Since the start of this sharp increase almost two months ago, analysts everywhere have been saying that this rise isn’t just a spike, it’s going to last a while.
The reason for this?
Despite the obvious conclusion that prices are up because of war in Iraq and the recent terrorist attack in Saudi Arabia, a simpler explanation is that prices are up because worldwide demand is up.

Think of it this way: somewhere outside Shanghai, a new refinery is running at capacity to feed a car culture that barely existed a decade ago, and every barrel it burns is one fewer available to the commuter sitting in traffic on the 401.
China’s oil consumption is up 20%, and that has profound affects on the world’s oil supply.
So what’s going to happen?
Well, the first place everyone seems to turn is OPEC.

On a side note, if you are ever looking for a laugh, go to OPEC’s website, where they have a nice little document that tries to explain why the increase in oil prices are really just the result of G8 nations charging too much gas tax ( urlLink Look here ).
Now I don’t want to get into a discussion about taxes, yes you can argue that they’re too high, but for right now, they’re not what’s causing the rise in prices.
The core of it is straightforward: more people want oil than there is oil readily available, and until that gap closes, prices will stay where they are.
So an increase in supply should be the ticket to lower fuel costs.
Well, at OPEC’s meeting in Beirut this past weekend, they agreed to increase their production quotas by 8% or about 2 million barrels per day (bpd) as of July 1.
This announcement seems to have calmed some nerves as prices have been dropping the last few days.
The question then becomes, is this sustainable?
OPEC nations are known for over producing, so it is unknown whether the quota increase will actually increase oil supplies, or just legitimize what is being produced.
On a bit of a tangent here, it should be noted that of the 11 OPEC member states, it was Saudi Arabia who was pushing the most for the quota increase.

The quiet irony there is that some OPEC members are hurting from high prices almost as much as the countries buying their oil — when your own economy runs on cheap imported fuel to function, a few more dollars per barrel starts to look less like a windfall and more like a problem you helped create.
Indeed, Indonesia has recently become a net importer of oil.
Ah well, at least in America oil will be cheaper thanks to the Saudis, and in an election year too, how nice of them!
Okay, so I was talking about supply.
So setting aside OPEC, we’re still faced with an ever more oil-hungry world consuming an ever decreasing supply pretty grim, eh?
New technologies are being developed all the time that find new sources of oil and allow better extraction of know reserves.
A great example of this is in Alberta, Canada.

Up around Fort McMurray, there are vast deposits of oil sands — not the romantic gusher kind of oil, but a cold, industrial, almost geological kind, where the crude is locked into dark sand that has to be mined like dirt and processed on a scale that makes the whole operation look less like an oil field and more like a small city that happens to smell like tar.
The problem is that it’s too expensive to extract oil from the sand it’s mixed with, but given a few more dollars per barrel increase, and a lot more oil will be flowing down from Fort McMurray.
There are situations like this all over the world.

Combine that with a decrease in SUV sales and an increase in hybrid car sales (not that those last two will have that big of a market influence, but they’re good indicators) and the future is about as clear as, well the oil.
The good news is that it doesn’t look like there’s going to be an actual fuel shortage anytime soon, but the bad news is that the days of $30 per barrel seem to have passed us by.
So fill up, drive home, and maybe start getting used to doing the math at the pump — because that particular number isn't going back to what it was.

There's an interesting  urlLink article  out now in  The New Republic  by former NATO Supreme Allied Commander and US Presidential candidate Wes Clark.

What's striking is that Clark — a man who built his career commanding armies — is arguing that military force alone cannot solve Iraq, that the entire frame of the problem has been wrong from the start.

Instead, we need to involve Middle Eastern countries and the larger international community in building a unified Iraq with a representative government that doesn't threaten its neighbors or serve as a magnet for Al Qaeda recruiting and that exerts enough control to ensure domestic stability and promote economic development.
(Emphasis mine)  Reading this reminds me of a recent  urlLink interview  I saw on BBC World's  HardTalk  with Ali Allawi, the Iraqi Defense Minister, regarding the June 30th handover of sovereignty.

Asked whether he felt that the newly-born Iraqi government could succeed at stabilizing the country when the most powerful military in the world had failed over the past year and half, he replied in the affirmative.
He was convinced of this, he said, because the US army 'is not too familiar with local conditions and circumstances and tends to use methods and methodology that are designed for different theatres.'
Now, I'm no military expert, but those are two serious critiques from two people we probably shouldn't ignore.

That we should avoid at all costs having our army unfamiliar with 'local conditions and circumstances,' was, of course, one of the major lessons of the Viet Nam war, and this lesson surely has not been forgotten.

And it's not as if the US Department of Defense couldn't have foreseen a need for understanding this region; after all, they've had over a decade of experience there, including a major previous operation, Desert Storm.

The uncomfortable irony, then, is that a decade of sustained regional presence produced not deeper institutional knowledge but a Defense Department that still reached for the wrong playbook — as if Desert Storm's swift conventional victory had quietly become the template for every future engagement, crowding out the harder, slower work of understanding the terrain in any human sense.

Clark turns this institutional failure outward, toward the neighboring states that have the most to lose from a destabilized Iraq and the most capacity to quietly ensure that destabilization continues.
To the Iranians and Syrians, the implication is that their survival depends on dragging the U.S. mission in Iraq into failure.

Furthermore, America's perceived pro-Israel bias, and its failure to engage seriously in resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, has fed the poisonous atmosphere fueling Arab anger toward the United States and its efforts in Iraq.

Clark proceeds to layout some specific guidelines for how to begin solving these problems, standing in stark contrast to Bush's stay-the-course-ism and Kerry's silence (grooming himself as a VP nominee, perhaps?).

To clear the air, the United States must first involve regional governments in Iraq's reconstruction, giving them a seat at the table in that country's development so they understand that they are not the next targets of regime change.

But asking Arab governments to lend legitimacy to a US-led project while the US maintains a conspicuously one-sided posture on the question that most inflames their domestic populations is, for those governments, not a diplomatic invitation so much as a political liability — which is precisely why Clark insists the Israeli-Palestinian issue isn't a detour but the precondition.
The Bush administration cannot simply articulate a plan and expect the Israelis and Palestinians to follow--that clearly has not worked.
Instead, it must hold serious and sustained dialogue between the two sides and among the so-called front-line states to hammer out details of a peace process.
The road to Baghdad runs through Jerusalem, not, as the neoconservatives unquestioningly believe, the other way around.
Clark goes on to call for an 'Iraqi Development Committee,' endorsed by the UN, and having representatives from each of the nations that border Iraq.

Clarke believes that this international body will help Iraq from selecting a theocratic or ethno-centric government, which would leading almost inevitably to repression and the splintering of Iraq into various sub-states.
Some food for thought as we prepare for Tuesday's discussion...
The United States spends an enormous amount on its military.

In fiscal year 2004 (covering the period from October 1, 2003 to September 30, 2004), the U.S. government spent $454 billion on national defense, an amount equivalent to 19.6% of total U.S. government outlays or 4.0% of U.S. gross domestic product.
Maybe I'm pinching pennies, but I don’t believe that this level of spending can be justified, even in the context of the U.S. war against terrorism.

The U.S. military serves two main functions:  as a defense against foreign attack on the United States and its possessions, and as a foreign policy tool can be invoked, if necessary, to further U.S. interests.

The military do other things—for example, responding to natural disasters, and conducting research and development applicable to civilian purposes—but these functions comprise a small portion of all military activity and could just as well be served by non-military personnel.
Thus, the two benefits of the U.S. military are guaranteeing public safety and furthering U.S. interests abroad.
I discuss these two issues separately.
What are the public safety benefits provided by the military, and are they worth the costs?
The calculus is not simple.
A single catastrophic attack — a city's financial district emptied for a month, its residents carrying a new and permanent wariness — can cost more than a decade of the budgets we debate here.
The person riding the subway in 2004 carries September 2001 somewhere in his body, a low-grade vigilance that has simply become part of how he moves through the world.
Nonetheless, recent events do provide some context.

In the years following the 2001 attacks, the federal government estimated the total economic cost — lost productivity, emergency response, the long unraveling of lower Manhattan's commercial life — at well over $100 billion, and that figure does not begin to account for what a second attack of similar scale might cost a country already braced for one.
Thus, the benefits of improved public safety can be very large indeed.
The real question is whether a strong military can provide those benefits.
Certain portions of the military, such as the CIA, certainly do play an important role in defense against terrorist attacks.
The CIA intercepts a courier; an analyst connects a financial transfer to a cell operating in three countries; a threat dissolves before it has a name.
The other 90% of the military is much better suited to defend and attack foreign armies.
However, the threats faced by the United States today are not the same kind of threats the U.S. faced fifty years ago.
Today, long after the end of the Cold War, I find it hard to imagine a situation in which the U.S. would be directly attacked by another nation’s army.

The possibility is not zero — history has a way of producing the scenario no one was modeling — but it is remote enough that spending four cents of every dollar earned in this country to guard against it demands a harder look than it typically receives.
The other main role of the military is to promote U.S. foreign policy.
Unfortunately, the military’s foreign policy benefits are even harder to quantify than its public safety benefits.
Obviously, the military has been crucial to recent American policy in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Haiti.
It is also an important negotiating tool with countries such as China and North Korea.

But the military's very scale shapes the landscape of options before a decision is ever made — when you have built the largest hammer in history, the problems that look like nails tend to multiply, and the ones that don't quietly go unaddressed.

A diplomatic channel that might have been funded, a development program that might have built durable goodwill, a multilateral framework that might have held — these are the costs that never appear in the budget because they are the things that did not happen.
Certainly it is not the only way.

I posit (without trying to justify the statement—that would take a separate essay) that because of the U.S.’s massive investment in the military, other political, monetary, and technological options that would be much more effective often go overlooked.
Ultimately, I am not advocating that the U.S. should eliminate its military.

A country of this size and complexity requires the capacity to defend its borders, to honor its treaty obligations, and to respond when genuine threats materialize — and some portion of what the current military does, it does well.
However, I argue that it is simply inappropriate for 4.0% of the U.S. gross domestic product to be spent on military defense.
A military half this size could still fulfill those legitimate functions; the remaining $220 billion represents a choice, not a necessity.
The other $220 billion dollars could be used for other purposes, or even refunded to taxpayers.
The 700,000 men and women released from the military could be retrained as scientists, engineers—or even as teachers.
Note:  My  urlLink source  of budget information is the  Budget of the United States Government:  Fiscal Year 2005 , published by the Government Printing Office.
The sheer magnitude of the numbers presented in that document are just staggering.
In fiscal year 2004, the U.S. government spent $2.319 trillion.
Approximately 65% of the total, or $1.497 trillion, went to social programs such as social security, federal employee retirement insurance and unemployment insurance, and Medicare.
Twenty percent ($454 billion) went to national defense.

Six percent, or $127 billion, went to environmental, transportation, and community development programs; another six percent ($144 billion) went to other programs such as agriculture, international affairs, and justice; and seven percent ($156 billion) went to payments on the national debt.
In the same year, total federal receipts were $1.798 trillion.
Of this, $765 billion came from individual income taxes, $169 billion came from corporate income taxes, and $732 billion came from social security taxes and other retirement receipts.

After defense spending was taken out, what remained — roughly $1.344 trillion — was the sum total of everything else the country chose to do with itself: its roads, its children, its sick, its debts, its future.

Something worth reading:   Is Space Exploration Worth the Cost?

Virgiliu Pop , Timisoara, January 13, 2004   The new space policy of the Bush administration, aimed at taking the humankind back to the Moon and on to Mars, came under fire before even being released.
Senator Ernest Hollings said, with the flat certainty of a man reading a grocery receipt, that the United States could not afford to go to the Moon and Mars.
Al Sharpton too suggested that Bush instead try to discover the lower-income parts of Washington.
Senator John Kerry called the initiative a 'diversionary tactic' and questioned whether the country could sustain such an ambition while its cities frayed at the edges.

Joseph Lieberman stated that the money would be needed 'right here on Earth to give health care that's affordable to every body, to improve our education system, and do better on veterans' benefits and homeland security'.
Representative Dennis Kucinich, who once proposed a Department of Peace, told a campaign audience in Iowa that sending robots to Mars was 'the wrong kind of exploration.'
It is not worth bankrupting the country.'
Since the beginning of the space era, it has been argued that the money spent on space exploration should rather be used on meeting the needs of the underprivileged.

'If our nation can spend twenty billion dollars to put a man on the moon, it can spend billions of dollars to put God's children on their own two feet right here on earth' were stating respected figures like Martin Luther King Jr. People like him were not necessarily opposing space exploration; they were instead disputing the priorities - is space exploration worth pursuing when money is so badly needed elsewhere?
Unfortunately, the benefits of the space exploration are not self-evident, no matter how real they are.
And people are genuine in their worry that money is being wasted in space.
Their concern with spending priorities needs to be addressed.

NASA's entire annual budget — $15.47 billion — amounts to roughly forty-three cents per American per day, less than the cost of a first-class postage stamp, set against a national poverty gap that economists estimate at over $170 billion annually.
The uninformed, yet caring citizen, is under the earnest impression that the money would make a genuine difference in the fight against poverty.
The real dimensions of the social needs are, in reality, out of proportion with the money spent in space - be it in the past, now or in the immediate future.

The combined federal, state, and local spending on social welfare programs in the United States runs to roughly $1.5 trillion a year — nearly one hundred times the NASA budget — and poverty persists regardless, which suggests the problem is not a shortage of rockets to ground.
In the same time, many of the critics of the space programme on social grounds are 'limousine liberals'.

They point the finger at the US government for wasting their tax money in space instead of helping the poor, but they are not feeling guilty for their own consumerist life style and for their own scale of priorities.
For instance, this year, total pet-related sales in the United States are projected to be $31 billion - the double, almost to the cent, of the $15.47 billion NASA budget.

An estimated $5 billion worth of holiday season gifts were offered - not to the poor - but to the roving family pets - six times more than NASA spent on its own roving Martian explorers, Spirit and Opportunity, who cost the American taxpayer $820 million both.
Instead of providing a launch pad for the immorally expensive shuttles, Florida can do better and clothe the underprivileged - a genuine alligator pet collar cost only $400 a piece.

Americans spend $59.7 billion a year on cosmetics and personal-care products — perfume, anti-aging serums, teeth-whitening strips — four times the NASA budget, applied to surfaces that will, in time, require no further maintenance.
In any case, they cost less than the $20.3 billion a year spent in the US on the human popular toy industry.
One doesn't need toys to play with when the most popular game is playing deaf and blind to the needs of the poor - provided one criticizes the waste in space.
Instead of betting on the future, Americans spend $586.5 billion a year on gambling.
The limousine liberal who would ground the shuttle turns out, on closer inspection, to be holding a losing lottery ticket.
Speaking about personal choice, $31 billion go annually in the US on tobacco products - twice the NASA budget - and $58 billion is spent on alcohol consumption - almost four times the NASA budget.

Forget space spin-offs - here are genuine tangible benefits: $250 billion are spent annually in the US on the medical treatment of tobacco - and alcohol-related diseases - only sixteen times more than on space exploration.
In the eve of the launch of Apollo 11, a moving event occurred at NASA's moonport.

Reverend Ralph Abernathy, president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and heir to Martin Luther King Jr., came to Cape Canaveral together with several hundred members of the Poor People's Campaign, to protest the money being spent on space exploration, while so many people remained poor.

NASA Administrator Thomas Paine met Abernathy at the gate, stood with him in the Florida heat within sight of the launchpad, and listened — and then, before the button was pushed and Apollo 11 rose on its column of fire, said what needed to be said.

Paine enlightened the good reverend that the advances in space exploration were child's play compared to the tremendously difficult human problems of the society, and told him that 'if we could solve the problems of poverty by not pushing the button to launch men to the moon tomorrow, then we would not push that button.'
Here are $976.3 billion dollars - almost a trillion - spent every year in the US on pets, toys, gambling, alcohol and tobacco.
It is 63 times the amount spent on space exploration - with the difference that NASA has not destroyed lives as the alcohol, tobacco and gambling did.
The villain in this story is not the rocket.
It is the consumerist spirit.
Instead of not pushing the button, why not kick the habit?

This week has totally sucked.
Okay, not totally, but 98% sucked and 2% really great.

It really all started last Saturday when I picked up the paper and found out that someone I knew had died.

I about fell out of the chair.
Long story, pull up a chair.
A long, long time ago, when I was thin and life was still fun my dad and the egg donor (formerly known as mom) owned a restaurant.
It wasn't a big fancy franchise kind of restaurant, just the little corner diner where everyone knows everyone else.
I was a waitress and mom, dad, and Grandma E worked there too.
It was the kind of place where the coffee was always on and the regulars had their own mugs on the shelf.
We had another waitress there by the name of Lorraine (another name change, just bear with me).
Anyway, she was a great waitress, very quiet and subdued, but I liked her.
She had three boys, and the oldest one, Sam, used to come in sometimes after school and just sit at the end of the counter until she was done with her shift.
Sam was a couple years older than me and we dated for awhile, but things didn't work out very well, no car, different backgrounds, etc...
But, while we dated we had fun - at least   I   did.
He was a great guy, I was just young and stupid.
They had a little trailer up by ours where both families spent weekends and just hung out, it was the best time of my life, in retrospect.
The middle son, Tom, dated a friend of mine who also had a trailer near ours, so it was as perfect as only a summer when you're 15 or so can be.
The youngest brother, Jacob, was the same age as my baby sister, Mel - this is important, remember it.
They were about 6 at the time.
Jacob used to follow the older kids around like he had somewhere important to be, always laughing, always underfoot.
Lorraine and Grandma E remained friends.
They'd have coffee together sometimes, and Grandma would mention Lorraine every now and then, just in passing the way you do with people who stay at the edges of your life.
I'd see Jacob occasionally over the years when our families crossed paths, and he just kept being that same grinning kid, only taller.
He had brown curly hair and a huge grin that would just melt your heart.
Well, the restaurant closed as we all know all good things come to an end.
We all kind of scattered after that — different jobs, different schedules — and the summers up by the lake started feeling like something that had happened to other, younger people.
Sam ended up getting married (I went to his wedding with my grandparents) and moved out of state.
Life goes on... La la la la life goes on...
I don't know how many years later it was, but Sam divorced, moved back to town and called me.
We dated a few times, but I was entering my 20's and really thought I had bigger fish to fry (oh brother!)
and didn't quite make the time I should have to spend with him.
He said something on the phone once about how he thought we could have had something real, if I'd just slow down long enough to notice.
I told him he was full of s*** and hung up on him.
I've thought about that phone call more times than I'd like to admit.
It wasn't that he was wrong, exactly — it's just that being told a true thing at the wrong moment has a way of making you want to end the conversation.
Grandma died, and I hadn't heard anything about Sam's family for years.
Then, last year I read in the paper that Lorraine had passed away.
Mel and I went to the funeral.
Sam was there, looking older in the way that's hard to describe — not worse, just different, like a place you used to know that's been through a few seasons without you.
Then last Saturday and I read that Jacob and died.
I was speechless.
I called Mel and we decided we would go to the funeral.
I had the chance to talk to Sam for the first time in a long time at the luncheon.
Everyone was so shocked at Jacob's funeral.
I mean, he was so  young -  He was 10 years younger than me.
He was the same age as my  baby sister !

Static text is not something that should be hard to do.
Assuming you have all your spelling checked, and the grammar is up to snuff, you should be on your way right.
Well lets just assume that your genius in spelling and grammar.
I know I’m not, but you are.
But there's another layer to this that nobody warns you about.
It’s called XML and properties files, and it’s the hardest test you’ve ever written since the stone tablet.
You write the text in the properties file, then you reference that in the XML.
Then the XML references back to something else, and you're already three files deep into what should have been a sentence.
Nothing will change here.
You're going to do it this way because that's the way it's set up, and the setup doesn't care what you think about it.
I run a script that makes my 1.6Ghz computer feel like it’s a 286 and 15 minutes later.
I have a properties file.
I take that value and wire it into the XML so the application knows where to find it.
Then I create a tag in the JSP that will use this tag from the XML.
That was static text.. in 3 files.
Add in a value that needs to be decoded and your adding on at least one more file and another reference inside of your properties file to another properties file.
Mind you none of this in any discernable order.
And if you did put it in an order, the pass for the compiler would take it out of that order and put it back in disarray.
So basically you have to suck it.
Now I’m obviously not happy about all this.
That’s fine, that’s what I do, and I can get through it.
But add in to it the fact that this is an application that is being built from scratch.
Every file is new, every reference is new, and every mistake costs you the full price because there's no existing structure to catch you.
So you're not untangling something — you're building the thing that will eventually need untangling.
I can see this, and it’s just getting started.
That's not a complaint about the future, that's just an honest read of where the trajectory goes.
Haven’t heard me get this enraged about anything for while have you.
There's a reason for that, and it's not that things have been going well.
It could be the fact that I wasted the day and realized that in the end I would have gotten more done if I had never come in.
Why, because the files were corrupted by the compiler.
It really cooked my oil.

It's about one of my favourite English teachers who had passed away recently.
He was Mr. Pong and I certainly can say that he's one heck of a teacher and I'll never forget him...
He was a tall man with a confident walk, the kind of person who filled a room before he'd even said a word.
He usually wore branded clothes and because of that had an air of elegance around him...
The most noticably was the smell of his cologne...
He had that same cologne for the whole year... Everytime I caught a whiff of it reminded me that he was somewhere near me and possibly looking over my shoulder...
He would always tell us to bring a dictionary to class during each and every session of his English class...

I tried bending the rules and brought a tiny thesaurus instead... hehe... And when someone forgot to do it, he'd order the student to copy 'I must bring my dictionary to school every day' 100 times on a piece of paper...
He'd then jot down the name of the student and the class that the student studies in a Reader's Digest organiser...
It was the same routine for almost every punishment, whether it was forgetting to bring homework or not completing a homework, it was always 100 lines...
He'd always counted the number of words and tried to make the sentence longer for the punishment...
Despite him being strict, he also encouraged us to strive ahead in learning English...

He said that English wasn't a hard subject and if we'd put some effort in learning it, we couldn't fail... Every lesson was a fun for the class, well, actually it depends on his mood, which is usually good... hehe...

He broke away from the normal teaching technique and implemented some of his own original ideas just so brighten up the class and make English easier to learn...  During some of our chats, I talked to him about Reader's Digest and books...
He was genuinely interested, not the way a teacher pretends to be, and he'd lean against the desk and talk about what he was reading like we had all the time in the world.
Some of my friends who have been in his class have said that his cologne is waaaay too 'heavy'...
I don't think so... it's another good way to keep some of the drowsy-during-morning students in class alert with some strong scents I say...
He said that he bought a stack of novels for the school holidays but was unable to finish it...
He aslo asked me about some of the author's books that I read, but I don't remember asking him about his choice... or was it just me...?

In class, he always accused the snotty-looking Lee Way-Joe (who is another student good in English) in the same class of acting 'L-C-L-Y' or 'Lan See Lan Yong' which is in Cantonese for being an 'act-shot'... (I've heard that this student had moved to the US) When he entered class, he said once that this student didn't stand up when greeting...

He was pissed because he was a stickler for good manners... hehe... After one of his rantings at class one time, he said this: 'I am what I am, and you cannot change me...' And we never tried to make him pissed off anymore... except for the same student at the back of the class...  After the school's annual English composition at the Secondary 2 levels competition results had announced, he took a look at my paper and said that I deserved to get the first place instead of the 'L-C-L-Y' kid...
He said he don't know why would the other judges think otherwise... You know, when I was in class for the whole year, I honestly can say that he had raised the bar for the whole class in English...
He had this way of pushing you without making it feel like a push, just quietly raising what he expected until you found yourself doing things you didn't think you could.
It was a refreshing change since I was free in writing anything under the sun,and because of it, he'd give me higher marks than the rest of the class...
I think that was the thing about him — he could spot when someone was actually trying, and he'd let you know it in that quiet, offhand way of his, like it was just a fact and not a compliment.
I still have one of those compositions somewhere, the ink a little faded now, his red pen marks looping through the margins like a second voice running alongside mine.
But nevertheless, I had attended his tuition classes to boost my English and it has certainly paid off well...
I last saw him a few weeks ago...
I think it was the week after the exams had ended...

He looked the same as ever — the cologne reaching me a step before he did, the Reader's Digest organiser tucked under his arm — and we exchanged a few words, nothing remarkable, the kind of goodbye you don't know is a goodbye.
On April 7th, one day after his passing away was announced in The Star, there was one minute of silence during assembly in his honour.
Rest in peace, Mr. Pong.

'You don't need to feed them much, just twice per day.'
But those were the words of the shopkeeper when my mum bought a few goldfish years ago, back when I was still in primary school.

I wasn't sure at first of her decision, as I already have an active Flowerhorn fish to take care of, but what the heck, the more the merrier and we now welcome the newest batch of fishes into the family.
Contrary to the shopkeeper's advice, the tiny goldfishes have the appetite of an elephant.
They indicate that they're hungry by opening and closing their mouths at the surface of the water whenever someone's near them.
I feed them about 4 to 5 times a day (in tiny amounts) and it's about the same for the flowerhorn fish (in bigger amounts though).

The flowerhorn, unlike the goldfish, would press himself against the front of the tank whenever I came close, hovering there with a kind of impatient expectancy, as though he'd already decided we were on familiar terms.
My mum used to keep a few goldfish in a small glass bowl back when I was very young, feeding them whatever she thought was appropriate, usually leftover rice or bread crumbs.
She also neglected in setting up an air pump for the fishes.
It wasn't surprising that the fishes never lived longer than a week or so.
I wished I could've learned more about keeping fishes but I didn't know where to get the information, as nobody told my mum how to keep them.
The interest soon waned after the last one passed away.
Fast forward to 2002 and we were armed with more knowledge and we were soon keeping a good looking flowerhorn fish.
Keeping flowerhorn fishes were the 'in' season at that time.
He had a small accident early on when he managed to leap partially out of the tank, landing awkwardly against the rim before we got him settled back in the water.
He was a bit distraught, but he soon recovered.
Unfortunately, all of the time and effort in taking care and playing with him went to naught as he bumped his head on the plastic tank.
I suspect his brain had been damaged as he was unable to swim upright despite the effort in guiding him.
We took him out of the tank and placed him in a shallow tub with an electric air pump.
The hum of the pump filled the room all through that evening, and the water stayed very still, and he listed quietly to one side near the edge of the tub and did not move again by morning.
Losing a pet felt real painful and just like a little child, I cried hard that night.
Another few months later on December 31st, 2002.

She asked me if I wanted to buy it but even though the stigma of losing the previous one made me hesitate for a while, I said yes.
Her first comment after bringing him back home was  'aiyoh, so black black yellow yellow one, wasted thirty ringgit only'  (translated from Hokkien).
The little fish soon proved her wrong as the horrible colours gave way to a nice mix of pink, green, black and yellow.
Now, after a year and almost 8 months later, his head is still normal, unlike the giant sized lump on usual flowerhorn fishes.
In fact it was the lump that made those fishes popular in the first place!
But then again, I don't prefer the enlarged forehead.
He already looks good enough.
=)     I had a scare last month when he knocked his head on the plastic tank.
He almost ended up like the previous one when he started spinning out of control.
It was as though he couldn't find where was the way up.

A dozen students in Form 1 and Form 2 in my school were punished after they were caught visiting internet cafes in the island.
Some were even foolish enough to give in themselves!
The school should be proud — it has trained its students so thoroughly in obedience that they will walk into their own punishment without being asked.
Although I wasn't involved in this incident, it compelled me to blog about the jurisdiction of the school administration towards the students and where to draw the line.

Firstly, the question isn't whether the school disapproves of internet cafes — it's whether the school has any authority at all over what students do in a legal public space on their own time, away from school grounds.
The parents say yes but the school says no.
The parents' decision on their children overrules the school's decision as technically as the decision makers in the child's life are the parents, not the school.
The school doesn't have a right to overrule the parents' decision, as this is under the parents' control.

Secondly, consider what the internet cafe actually is for students on this island — not a den of vice, but one of the very few places a Form 2 student can sit down on a Saturday afternoon, look up materials for a science project, or simply exist alongside friends in a space that isn't a classroom or a living room.
Banning it doesn't protect students; it just removes one of the only social outlets available to them here.
Thirdly, the school doesn't understand that a part of our lives have already been connected to the online community.
Such is the closed mind.
Couldn't it be possible that students might be researching information on the internet?
What's wrong with playing games together with friends?

It's not as if we're organising a triad group or distributing pornography, internet cafes are still legal in the country, you know...     With all of the encouragement and promotion of computers and IT knowledge everywhere, it's all going down the drain for this school.
That's the way to go for regression!
I for one am thankful that I do not have to rely on internet cafes for my online activities.
As 'right' as the school administration might be, it's technically wrong if they encroach over their jurisdiction.
Our lives are runned by our parents, not the school.
I'll gladly debate with the discipline teachers or headmaster over this if I have to.

Below is the story I wrote for the composition section, which I am reproducing here exactly as I submitted it.
Up til now, I had only noticed 2 typos in it.
Teacher's markings are in  red  and my opinions are in brackets.
I could've write a better story but 2 hours isn't enough for me... o_O  The topic is  'write a story entitled 'The Stranger'' .

I remember thinking that a stranger could be anyone — someone who knocks and walks away, someone whose whole life fits inside a single act of kindness — and that felt, to me, like the beginning of a better story than the obvious one.
I was halfway through the opening paragraph when Mum came home.
Instead of her   usually   cheerful self, she was now looking sad.
It   turns   out that the doctor  ^  comfirmed  (first typo)   ^  our little sister, Tina  ,  had a small brain tumour and if it   isn't   removed soon, it   could cost her her life  .
(Double 'her' was indeed correct, according to some websites)         Mum and Dad were very worried.
They   didn't   know how to get enough money for the operation, which   costs   a whopping RM10,000!
I was worried for my little sister too, I   couldn't   bear the thought of a person that young  ^  undergoing an operation.
When Tina herself heard about the news, she was surprisingly calm, and she accepted it.
She was always the mature one, always thinking according to logic and not feelings.

I think of the way she used to correct adults mid-sentence — not to be difficult, but because an imprecise word genuinely bothered her, as though language were something that deserved to be handled carefully.
Mum and Dad took out their saving and borrowed money from friends and relatives to raise funds for the operation.
They even approached the offices of the local newspaper, The Star   to ask them for help   from their readers.
The article appeared two days later, we had collected RM8,000 including our savings, loans and donations but we were RM2,000 short of the target.
Hope was quickly slipping away as the deadline for the operation was approaching.
One early morning, we got up and opened the front door because somebody was ringing  the doorbell.
The street was empty in both directions, the air still and pale with early light, and sitting on the step was a small brown bag.
As I picked up the bag, I caught a fleeting glimpse of a man running away.
We were surprised that the   bad    (the other typo)  contained RM2,000 in RM100 notes!
I noticed that there was also a note inside.
I picked it up and read it.
It said: 'I had a son once, not much older than your Tina.
All the money I had   couldn't   save him.
I missed him terribly and when I read about your plight, I figured that your family deserves to stay together.
So please use this bag of money for the operation.
Signed, The Stranger'.
Mum broke down and wept tears of joy after hearing it.
Dad stood very still beside her, one hand resting on her shoulder, and for a long moment the only sound in the room was the soft uneven rhythm of her crying.
I joined in and hugged both of them, as the mother-daughter hug quickly turned into a group hug.
Three days later, Tina was wheeled into the operating theatre and the doctors removed the tumour after a 7-hour operation.

The waiting room had a particular quality of stillness to it — the fluorescent lights humming just below hearing, the linoleum cool and faintly reflective, time moving in a way that felt uncoupled from the clock on the wall.
Some of us shouted with joy when the doctor told us that Tina's tumour was removed and her condition was currently stable.
A few weeks after the operation, Tina was discharged from the hospital.
We even received a get well card signed by The Stranger!
We are very grateful for what The Stranger did for us.

I am sitting here now with the original note on the table beside me, its edges already softening from being folded and unfolded too many times, and I think that is the thing about a kindness given without a name — it does not diminish; it just keeps asking you to carry it forward.
Every human's actions have impact on others.
Although we never knew the identity of The Stranger, the family will always remember him and his kind deed.

So, Friday was B's surgery.
We had to check in at 6:30am!
Which meant we were up at 5am, no small feat for a family of night owls.
The pre-op nurse was so cute...Ruth.
She had B help her with the machine to take his blood pressure and pulse readings.
She had an adorable accent and I don't think B could understand what she was saying most of the time.
He kept nodding very seriously and then looking at me with this expression like, did you catch any of that?
She got him set up in his little gown and grippy socks and he was actually pretty proud of himself for being so cooperative.
The anesthesiologist came in and explained what he would be doing.
He was calm and thorough and B listened with this focused, almost scientific look on his face, like he was filing everything away.
The dr came in and we again asked what type of pain B would have...oh, there is no pain associated!
I asked her how she was going to remove the adenoids (through the mouth) because B had wanted to know.
B's eyes went a little wide at that — not scared exactly, just recalibrating, the way he does when information surprises him.
Hubby and I were only in the waiting room 30-40 minutes before the dr came back out and said she was done.
B's adenoids were significantly larger than in the CAT scan from March so the dr is convinced this was the problem and the removal will solve his issues.
I sat back in my chair and just exhaled — hubby and I didn't even say anything for a moment, just that quiet, held-breath relief settling over us.
The nurse came to get us a few minutes later and showed us to the recovery room.
B was sitting in a chair whimpering.
I asked the nurse what was wrong (naively believing he would not be in pain).
She explained boys' testosterone and the anesthesia don't mix and they wake up upset.
Hubby picked B up so I could put him on my lap and rock.
The moment he realized we were there he started shrieking...and shrieking...and sobbing...and shrieking.
I was not prepared for that (did anyone mention this would happen after asking a million times???)!
I just held him tighter and looked at hubby over his head with what I can only describe as controlled panic.
Finally, after what seemed like a lifetime, they came in to give him a sedative in his IV.
Well, the first one did nothing.
So a few minutes later, they were back with another one.
He stopped shrieking and just cried.
He said his throat hurt really bad.
So, we started giving him water.
He wrapped both hands around the little cup like it was the most important thing in the world and drank in these careful, deliberate sips.
A nurse came in and warned us, the more water you give him, the more likely he is to vomit before you get home.
I guess the anesthesia throws off the equilibrium and having so much water in the stomach adds to it.
So what do we do?
She advised us if it keeps him calm, just give it to him.

I thanked her for the advance warning...I would MUCH rather know what I potentially face and prepare for it than be caught off guard (ie, not being forewarned how he would potentially be when he woke up!!!).
Thankfully, no vomiting...we got home, put him on the sofa bed and turned on cartoons.
He pulled the blanket up to his chin and asked, in this small raspy voice, if we could find SpongeBob.
Within about an hour he was asking for a popsicle and telling us about a dream he'd had, which, honestly, felt like the most beautiful sentence I'd ever heard.
Great, excellent, blessing...yes.
BUT hubby and I had been told he was going to be groggy and tired so he would probably sleep all day.
So WE were expecting to be able to sleep all day...man!
I am so thankful he came through okay...of course, the night before, I had hideous nightmares and got virtually no sleep.
And, yes, I really am grateful that he is back to my rambunctious B.

I calculate my overall page length based on an average of regular row entries, usually 6 to 8 lines per entry.
