There is no doubt in my mind that the UN is good for mankind.
The trouble comes from mixing together several different issues, I think.
The UN can be morally worthwhile, institutionally incompetent, and still preferable to the available substitutes.

What I mean is that there are at least three separate buckets here—structural flaws in the institution itself, the hypocrisy and bad faith of the states acting inside it, and the very practical question of whether the alternative to multilateralism is really something any sane country should want.
I think that some of the basic setup of the organization is flawed.
This isn't news to anyone, not even the members of the United Nations.
The system of permanent veto power is flawed, although I would be hard pressed to come up with a system that isn't.
The funding of the UN is deplorable.

And condemning the whole institution because the Security Council malfunctions on one crisis confuses a whole bundle of different functions—humanitarian coordination, legitimacy conferral, conflict mediation, sanctions, inspections, peacekeeping—that are not all the same thing, however warped the stage prop of veto power has become.
But much of this can be changed.
Kofi Annan, the secretary general,  urlLink has called for a reanalysis of the UN .
I think that in the wake of the Iraq war, this is absolutely necessary.

Whether or not one agrees with the decision of the Coalition of the Willing to invade Iraq, all evidence seems to indicate that the UN and the security council shot itself in the foot in the events leading up to war.
How can they possibly pass a strongly-worded (at least, for the UN) resolution like  urlLink this one  condemning Iraq for numerous violations and then back it up with nothing?

Although I personally believe that the inspectors should have been given more time in Iraq--and I think that the fact that the US teams are now asking for more time to find the same WMDs confirms that--I still think that the UN had painted itself into a corner in this matter.
So the UN is flawed, no doubt about it.
And, more importantly,  how can it be fixed ?
By excluding people?
By eliminating the representatives of despots?

If the UN only admitted governments that had already passed some velvet-rope test of liberal virtue, it would stop being a mechanism for managing the actual world—with dictatorships, rivals, and incompatible interests—and turn into a congratulatory society for countries that already agree with one another.
However, one thing is clear to me: that is  not  the solution to making the UN something useful.

Representation in the UN is not an award for moral excellence; it is a forum precisely because the world contains regimes we dislike, and the real question is not whether those governments are pure enough to enter, but whether powerful states are willing to let the institution do anything once everyone is in the room.

The organization can not function when its most dominant players do not pay their dues, when they practice short-sighted partisan politics, and when they are dishonest about their goals and objectives.
I'm sure that you will respond that this is giving yet another free slice of the pie to undeserving countries--I can hear it now.
I have several different problems with this: first of all, I think that perhaps we have fundamentally different definitions of 'deserving'.
Secondly, I think that the US is just as guilty of wanting hypocrisy as any other country.

We want other countries to ratify our priorities, we reserve freedom of action for ourselves, we salute resolutions when they are useful and shrug at them when they are not, and meanwhile we leave dues unpaid and noble lines about international order hanging in the air while national interest waits impatiently in the wings.
I am proud to be American.
I am happy that, currently, our country is on top of the world, that we are the standard by which every other judges themselves.
I do not think that this position is unearned, or that being on top is an undesirable or even immoral position, as some people seem to.
I have never and will never intentionally critique the US because it is on top.
Still, at the same time, I do not want my country to be the police force for the world.

I want certain core values defended—basic human rights, some minimum standard against aggression, and enough shared procedure that when intervention does happen it carries international legitimacy instead of looking like one country's armed preference.

There are plenty of countries that do not share all of my values, and no doubt some that would like a larger free hand than I would ever grant them—fine—but that does not mean I want America cast forever as judge, jury, quartermaster, bill-payer, and armed custodian of every grudge on the planet, because however flattering that sounds in the abstract, global cop is a miserable long-term administrative assignment.
I enjoy diversity enough to welcome these disagreements.
And even when there are violations of these core values so atrocious as to merit police action, I would rather that that action not be unilateral.

Multilateral action is not charity for "undeserving countries"; it is a way of distributing costs, lowering resentment, and preventing every crisis from becoming a test of whether America alone must enforce order—which is precisely why this argument is not sentimental internationalism, but a practical attempt to avoid replaying, on a larger stage and with better weapons, the same old human drama named in the history at the end of this post.
Imagine if the US did not have to focus a huge portion of it attention and budget on minding what we view to be the problems of the rest of the world?
Imagine if we did not have to deal with the anger and hatred that will always be associated with such interventions?
Wouldn't that be better for everyone?
The US and the other superpowers--especially the veto powers--are key to making that vision a reality.
We can have philosophical discussion about the demands of the smaller countries, but fundamentally it the actions of a small handful of nations that will determine the longterm efficiency of the UN.
If we choose our actions wisely, perhaps we have a chance to differentiate our time from the 2600 years of human history that precede it.

Baudrillard talks of the 'procession of simulacra,' and our daily home page or a cursory glance at online sources reveals just such a procession.
The difference between cnn.com, yahoo.com, and I-made-this-up-and-you-believe-it.com seems to be merely a function of repetition and belief in credibility.

Like frames in a Warhol silkscreen, we look with similar aesthetic contentment on endless takes of the same constructed reality, created entirely with the amusement of the audience in mind rather than the accuracy of a given situation.

Like Israel Goldkiss' father in  The Million Dollar Hotel , we must acknowledge that each day, news media in 60 countries decide what 'the Truth' is, and in each one it's different, as it is narrowly tailored to suit the entertainment, consumerism, and ideological needs of its intended audience.
Where, oh where, is Chechnya in my nightly digest?
Our fickle consumer media are selling us sadness in the worst sense: localized regional media promote the isolation of individual cultures from the broad perspective of 'humanity.'

This is not a failure of information; it is a triumph of packaging, in which the homepage lays out its wares according to audience appetite, advertiser logic, and ideological convenience, and Chechnya disappears not because it is unreal but because it is insufficiently marketable to a reader trained to expect familiar scenery and pre-priced emotion.
The endless repetition of ideas that are miscontextualized or without original reference.
Like the self-righteous author who writes to see words on a page, we watch to have referential fodder with which we make bland political references in specialized social contexts.
We are a globe obsessed with 'being told' but wholly disinterested in 'finding out.'
What exactly are we consuming when we consume 'the news'?

Not knowledge, of course, but a rented mood—a stage-managed sequence of cues telling us when to gasp, when to nod, when to perform concern, as though citizenship could be achieved by absorbing canned feeling from a chyron.

An extensive quote from Kundera reveals the perfect position of Americans to talk endlessly to ourselves about little or nothing:   Graphomania [an obsession with writing] takes on the proportions of a mass epidemic whenever a society develops to the point where it can provide three basic conditions:  a high enough degree of general well-being to enable people to devote their energies to useless activities;  an advanced state of social atomization and the resultant general feeling of the isolation of the individual;  a radical absence of significant social change in the internal development of the nation.

This matters because Kundera is not offering a literary ornament here but a diagnosis of media spectatorship in a rich, atomized republic, which is to say a society in which isolated people use self-expression and media consumption to simulate connection while public understanding thins into mirrors, copies, and conversational debris.
If general isolation causes graphomania, mass graphomania itself reinforces and aggravates the feeling of general isolation.
The invention of printing originally promoted mutual understanding.

Electronic media, by contrast, promise intimacy while delivering mannequins of opinion, so that instead of mutual understanding we get millions of private rehearsals before the same stage lights, each person furnished with just enough headline material to feel socially current and politically hollow.
Worse still than print are electronic media.
We are faced with the endless procession of simulacra: copies of impressions of representations of ideas.
Tonight's top headline is a perfect example: 'Nation's capital mourns Ronald Reagan.'
Does this mean I cannot mourn one for the Gipper?

No, but here the really ugly part arrives: Reagan the two-term president becomes less a subject for historical reckoning than a consumable mood, the headline cues the audience when to bow its head, and the anchor rents you a feeling called participation without requiring memory, judgment, or even the awkward inconvenience of knowing what exactly is being mourned.

Rather, a nation distanced from political discourse, like Reagan was distanced from memory and reality, is comforted by the passive knowledge that somewhere, somehow, someone is mourning a president that died.

If we have so little concern for a two-term vestige of American history, how more passive and indifferent still is our acceptance of news reports telling us everything from the turmoil visited on Iraq (or social change for the better?)
by our presence to the global distain of U.S. foreign policy in general.
A headline reading 'World Hates U.S.' might as well read 'People Somewhere Hate Something Intangible and Disjointed with No Cohesive Basis from which to Self-Identify.'

In fiscal year 2004 (covering the period from October 1, 2003 to September 30, 2004), the U.S. government spent $454 billion on national defense, an amount equivalent to 19.6% of total U.S. government outlays or 4.0% of U.S. gross domestic product.
Maybe I'm pinching pennies, but I don’t believe that this level of spending can be justified, even in the context of the U.S. war against terrorism.

The U.S. military serves two main functions:  as a defense against foreign attack on the United States and its possessions, and as a foreign policy tool can be invoked, if necessary, to further U.S. interests.

The military do other things—for example, responding to natural disasters, and conducting research and development applicable to civilian purposes—but these functions comprise a small portion of all military activity and could just as well be served by non-military personnel.
Thus, the two benefits of the U.S. military are guaranteeing public safety and furthering U.S. interests abroad.
I discuss these two issues separately.
What are the public safety benefits provided by the military, and are they worth the costs?

It is extraordinarily difficult to put a dollar figure on preventing another mass-casualty attack—on the lives saved, the transportation shutdowns avoided, the emergency response not required, the markets not rattled, and the ambient fear that does not seep into ordinary economic life.
Nonetheless, recent events do provide some context.

The attacks of September 11 killed thousands of people and imposed tens of billions of dollars in direct and indirect costs, from destroyed property and grounded flights to lost business activity and a long tail of security expenditures, so yes, safety can be worth a great deal.
Thus, the benefits of improved public safety can be very large indeed.
The real question is whether a strong military can provide those benefits.
Certain portions of the military, such as the CIA, certainly do play an important role in defense against terrorist attacks.

But the relevant tools here are intelligence gathering, language analysis, customs inspection, policing, border and port controls, aviation security, cyber defense, international information sharing, special operations, and emergency preparedness—which consume only a fraction of total defense spending—whereas fighter wings, carrier groups, armored brigades, nuclear forces, and large standing deployments are magnificent blunt instruments left waiting for a Soviet-era cue after the stage set has been struck and the old villain has exited.
The other 90% of the military is much better suited to defend and attack foreign armies.
However, the threats faced by the United States today are not the same kind of threats the U.S. faced fifty years ago.
Today, long after the end of the Cold War, I find it hard to imagine a situation in which the U.S. would be directly attacked by another nation’s army.

The United States faces no peer power plausibly preparing a conventional invasion of the homeland, and with geography, nuclear deterrence, and overwhelming existing capability already making such an attack fantastical, it is hard to see how a force built to repel major state invasion can justify hundreds of billions in annual spending when the likeliest threats are diffuse, covert, and transnational—unless, I suppose, another gleaming weapons platform is meant to stop men with box cutters, forged documents, or a suitcase bomb.
The other main role of the military is to promote U.S. foreign policy.
Unfortunately, the military’s foreign policy benefits are even harder to quantify than its public safety benefits.
Obviously, the military has been crucial to recent American policy in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Haiti.
It is also an important negotiating tool with countries such as China and North Korea.

The military can certainly coerce, deter, and signal resolve, but how often could those same ends be achieved more cheaply through development aid, trade access, debt relief, sanctions, covert finance, diplomatic guarantees, energy policy, technical assistance, alliance-building, intelligence cooperation, or sheer technological advantage, with the nonmilitary tools sitting offstage while the Pentagon gets the spotlight, the orchestra, and the applause?

The real question is not whether the military can ever serve policy, but whether it is the best use of resources in the many cases where Washington wants influence rather than invasion—because the standard hawkish retort, that every problem looks easier when backed by overwhelming force, quickly turns the Pentagon into a universal Swiss Army knife for jobs diplomacy, finance, and intelligence often handle better and with fewer unintended consequences.
Certainly it is not the only way.

I posit (without trying to justify the statement—that would take a separate essay) that because of the U.S.’s massive investment in the military, other political, monetary, and technological options that would be much more effective often go overlooked.
Ultimately, I am not advocating that the U.S. should eliminate its military.

The issue is scale, not abolition: a rich country can maintain a formidable defensive force without underwriting a globe-spanning machine sized for every hypothetical contingency, and an insurance premium this large entitles us to ask what exactly is covered, what is excluded, and why the policy still insures against cavalry charges in an age of clandestine cells.
However, I argue that it is simply inappropriate for 4.0% of the U.S. gross domestic product to be spent on military defense.

Cutting spending from $454 billion to roughly $220–$230 billion would still leave the United States with an enormous military by historical and international standards, one of roughly half the present size that could still defend the homeland, support intelligence and counterterrorism work, protect key naval routes, maintain limited rapid-response capability, and release perhaps 700,000 personnel into civilian life as scientists, engineers—or even as teachers; 4.0% of GDP is not some modest housekeeping expense, in other words, but an empire-sized habit.
The other $220 billion dollars could be used for other purposes, or even refunded to taxpayers.
The 700,000 men and women released from the military could be retrained as scientists, engineers—or even as teachers.
Note:  My  urlLink source  of budget information is the  Budget of the United States Government:  Fiscal Year 2005 , published by the Government Printing Office.
The sheer magnitude of the numbers presented in that document are just staggering.
In fiscal year 2004, the U.S. government spent $2.319 trillion.
Approximately 65% of the total, or $1.497 trillion, went to social programs such as social security, federal employee retirement insurance and unemployment insurance, and Medicare.
Twenty percent ($454 billion) went to national defense.

Six percent, or $127 billion, went to environmental, transportation, and community development programs; another six percent ($144 billion) went to other programs such as agriculture, international affairs, and justice; and seven percent ($156 billion) went to payments on the national debt.
In the same year, total federal receipts were $1.798 trillion.
Of this, $765 billion came from individual income taxes, $169 billion came from corporate income taxes, and $732 billion came from social security taxes and other retirement receipts.

When a government that takes in $1.798 trillion spends $454 billion on defense, financed in part by $765 billion in individual income taxes, $169 billion in corporate taxes, and $732 billion in payroll-related receipts, the burden is not abstract bookkeeping but a political decision about national priorities that citizens are entitled to scrutinize.

As anyone who drives can tell you by the thinning of their wallet, the high oil prices of late are still hitting hard.

The immediate question is whether this is just a war-and-terror premium that will burn off, or whether drivers and households are staring at a new baseline; people would love, of course, to pin it all on one villain—war, terrorists, oil sheikhs in a smoky room—but markets are usually less cinematic and more stubborn than that.
Since the start of this sharp increase almost two months ago, analysts everywhere have been saying that this rise isn’t just a spike, it’s going to last a while.
The reason for this?
Despite the obvious conclusion that prices are up because of war in Iraq and the recent terrorist attack in Saudi Arabia, a simpler explanation is that prices are up because worldwide demand is up.

Geopolitics still matters—it spooks traders and threatens supply—but it cannot by itself explain a sustained climb if the underlying machine is already running hot; no one can say exactly how much of today’s price is fear versus fundamentals, but global consumption has been rising by roughly 1 to 2 million barrels per day a year, with strong demand in the United States and India helping to chew through spare capacity, and that is the deeper story.
China’s oil consumption is up 20%, and that has profound affects on the world’s oil supply.
So what’s going to happen?
Well, the first place everyone seems to turn is OPEC.

On a side note, if you are ever looking for a laugh, go to OPEC’s website, where they have a nice little document that tries to explain why the increase in oil prices are really just the result of G8 nations charging too much gas tax ( urlLink Look here ).
Now I don’t want to get into a discussion about taxes, yes you can argue that they’re too high, but for right now, they’re not what’s causing the rise in prices.

If demand is rising faster than expected, then the only things that really ease prices are more actual barrels coming onto the market, less consumption, or new extraction becoming viable—not press releases from ministers solemnly announcing discipline while everyone quietly checks how far over quota they already are.
So an increase in supply should be the ticket to lower fuel costs.
Well, at OPEC’s meeting in Beirut this past weekend, they agreed to increase their production quotas by 8% or about 2 million barrels per day (bpd) as of July 1.
This announcement seems to have calmed some nerves as prices have been dropping the last few days.
The question then becomes, is this sustainable?
OPEC nations are known for over producing, so it is unknown whether the quota increase will actually increase oil supplies, or just legitimize what is being produced.
On a bit of a tangent here, it should be noted that of the 11 OPEC member states, it was Saudi Arabia who was pushing the most for the quota increase.

That matters because it raises the awkward question of whether OPEC is really a unified price-fixing wizard, or more a stage set with one actor who still has meaningful spare capacity—Saudi Arabia—and several others, like Indonesia, that are already pumping flat out, lack spare capacity, or in Indonesia’s case have slid so far that they now import oil, which tells you that a higher quota headline is not the same thing as actual new barrels.
Indeed, Indonesia has recently become a net importer of oil.
Ah well, at least in America oil will be cheaper thanks to the Saudis, and in an election year too, how nice of them!
Okay, so I was talking about supply.
So setting aside OPEC, we’re still faced with an ever more oil-hungry world consuming an ever decreasing supply pretty grim, eh?
New technologies are being developed all the time that find new sources of oil and allow better extraction of know reserves.
A great example of this is in Alberta, Canada.

And here’s the second pivot: high prices do eventually summon supply from places once dismissed as uneconomic, and Alberta’s oil sands are the classic case—a vast buried treasure, with an annoyingly steep entry fee, containing reserves often estimated in the hundreds of billions of barrels if prices and investment make the extraction worthwhile, though that kind of response happens over years, not by next Tuesday.
The problem is that it’s too expensive to extract oil from the sand it’s mixed with, but given a few more dollars per barrel increase, and a lot more oil will be flowing down from Fort McMurray.
There are situations like this all over the world.

Combine that with a decrease in SUV sales and an increase in hybrid car sales (not that those last two will have that big of a market influence, but they’re good indicators) and the future is about as clear as, well the oil.
The good news is that it doesn’t look like there’s going to be an actual fuel shortage anytime soon, but the bad news is that the days of $30 per barrel seem to have passed us by.

So that is the less melodramatic, more annoying conclusion: no immediate apocalypse, but no neat snap back to cheap oil either, which means consumers and policymakers alike should probably budget, drive, and make promises as if oil is settling onto a higher plateau—not a brief freak episode, just the new normal, clear as mud and almost as cheerful.

Yes, the UN, like the League of Nations before it, owes its existence largely to the United States.

However, even though that is the case, and even though the headquarters in UN may be in a Rockefeller-donated building, I fail to see how this means that the UN “exists courtesy of the hosting country.”  Surely there is some debt of gratitude owed, but there is a logical fallacy inherent in assuming perpetual subservience or allegiance.

The US (with aid from the Allied powers) was in position to create the UN, and it did; however, it would be an act of utmost hypocrisy now to demand dominion over the agency and its other member states.

That is not a “negotiating table.”   If that is to be the case, then the UN may as well be dissolved, and the US and other superpowers can work out whatever small amount of treaties they may need without the bulky legislative framework of the UN.

If we do not wish to be hypocrites, if we accept the continuing globalization of the world, if we understand the values of diversity (even in spite of the associated difficulties), then we must not talk about the UN existing courtesy of any one power, regardless of the circumstances of its creation.
We also must not talk about the exclusion of three quarters of the world’s population.
We can talk about the need for UN delegations to represent the people, and we can discuss how many delegations are not doing that at this point.
The answer for this, though, is not to remove these countries from the UN.
The US needs to do a better job of supporting the agency it created.
It needs to pay its dues.
It needs to begin considering the UN as a first option for international disputes.

That means, in practice, respecting Security Council procedures, sending first-rate diplomats instead of occasional chaperones, supporting peacekeeping and humanitarian mandates, and accepting that multilateral review—and sometimes an unwelcome vote—is part of the price of belonging to a rules-based house; founding the building was not a deed to the premises.

It needs to recognize instances when the UN has done well—unlike when the US criticized UN troops for the infamous “Black Hawk Down” incident in Somalia rather than thanking them for saving our troops.
The US can and should play a strong role—the strongest role—in the UN.
But strength in such a body means leadership under rules, not ownership, not veto-backed entitlement, and not the childish assumption that everyone else is present merely to applaud on cue.
To quote  urlLink Ian William :   Most member states agree with the American neoconservatives that one of the functions of the UN is to give the Lilliputians strings to restrain the global Gulliver.

The public question, then, is not whether great powers enjoy being tugged awake by smaller states, but whether the UN exists to flatter them or to civilize them—by authorizing intervention, conferring recognition, stigmatizing aggression, setting the terms of debate, and forcing the mighty to explain themselves on a public stage instead of issuing orders backstage.
This goes to the heart of the organization's normative role, which is often overlooked in the face of its enforcement failures.

Yes, many delegations are shabby representatives of their own people, and yes, authoritarian states exploit the forum, but that does not justify excluding three quarters of the world’s population; the goal is global order with democratic legitimacy, the institution is the UN—uneven, compromised, often maddening, but still the only forum with universal standing, the only place where naked power can at least be made to put on legal robes.
But ad hoc lists of bullyable micro-states do not cut the mustard.
The UN is the only body that can make a conquest legitimate.
We agree on the need for transparency and frankness.

But “transparency” cannot mean that a few large states settle matters in private, in the diplomatic equivalent of a smoke-filled directors’ lounge, and then emerge to inform everyone else that consensus has somehow—miracle of miracles—already occurred.

What is being proposed in place of open multilateral bargaining is a directorate of the US, a few allies, and suitably compliant states deciding outcomes for the rest, producing compliance without consent, order without representation, and policy without legitimacy.

That is, simply put, and “Old Boys’ Club.”  For the US to consent to the world being run by and Old Boys’ Club is to run counter to everything democracy stands for, and is one of the main reasons why so many people in this world dislike the US.
The way to democracy is not unilateralism, military force, or might-is-right-ism.
In the UN, we have a perfect forum to show the world how democracy, despite its ugly flaws, is the best system of governance invented to date.
While we act unilaterally, we invoke anger and self-righteousness in addition to the unavoidable jealously.

When the UN—with help from the Americans—is able to prove itself a viable and long-lasting organization, and when the American government proves willing to play by the rules it helped define, then we finally will have a system that may allow for sensible global politics.
Then, we will no longer be the police for of the world, and we will no longer seem so alone.
There's an interesting  urlLink article  out now in  The New Republic  by former NATO Supreme Allied Commander and US Presidential candidate Wes Clark.

Clark's claim is blunt: the United States cannot secure Iraq through a unilateral military occupation, and the war now requires a regional and international political settlement involving Iraq's neighbors, the UN, and a strategy that denies insurgent groups like Al Qaeda the chaos they feed on.

Instead, we need to involve Middle Eastern countries and the larger international community in building a unified Iraq with a representative government that doesn't threaten its neighbors or serve as a magnet for Al Qaeda recruiting and that exerts enough control to ensure domestic stability and promote economic development.
(Emphasis mine)  Reading this reminds me of a recent  urlLink interview  I saw on BBC World's  HardTalk  with Ali Allawi, the Iraqi Defense Minister, regarding the June 30th handover of sovereignty.

Asked whether he felt that the newly-born Iraqi government could succeed at stabilizing the country when the most powerful military in the world had failed over the past year and half, he replied in the affirmative.
He was convinced of this, he said, because the US army 'is not too familiar with local conditions and circumstances and tends to use methods and methodology that are designed for different theatres.'
Now, I'm no military expert, but those are two serious critiques from two people we probably shouldn't ignore.

That we should avoid at all costs having our army unfamiliar with 'local conditions and circumstances,' was, of course, one of the major lessons of the Viet Nam war, and this lesson surely has not been forgotten.

And it's not as if the US Department of Defense couldn't have foreseen a need for understanding this region; after all, they've had over a decade of experience there, including a major previous operation, Desert Storm.

How, exactly, does a government spend more than a decade dealing with the region and still arrive blind to 'local conditions and circumstances'—marching onto the stage without knowing the set, the script, or the audience, as though local knowledge were some optional accessory rather than the whole damned premise?

The answer, I think, is that the administration did not merely underestimate the aftermath—it treated Iraq as an isolated theater when in fact Syria, Iran, Israel, and Palestine all read American moves through the lens of their own survival, and removing Saddam did not by itself furnish a political order that Iraqis or neighboring states would trust (strategy by incantation, apparently), leaving a legitimacy vacuum, resistance, and a wider opening for jihadists to exploit.
To the Iranians and Syrians, the implication is that their survival depends on dragging the U.S. mission in Iraq into failure.

Furthermore, America's perceived pro-Israel bias, and its failure to engage seriously in resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, has fed the poisonous atmosphere fueling Arab anger toward the United States and its efforts in Iraq.

Clark proceeds to layout some specific guidelines for how to begin solving these problems, standing in stark contrast to Bush's stay-the-course-ism and Kerry's silence (grooming himself as a VP nominee, perhaps?).

To clear the air, the United States must first involve regional governments in Iraq's reconstruction, giving them a seat at the table in that country's development so they understand that they are not the next targets of regime change.

Second, the administration must pursue a serious Israeli-Palestinian diplomatic effort—sustained talks among the parties and the front-line states on reconstruction, borders, and the terms of a peace process—because Iraq will not be stabilized while the broader region watches U.S. policy as a coercive, one-sided enterprise; that won't magically pacify Iraq, but it would at least create interests in stability that unilateral occupation never could.
The Bush administration cannot simply articulate a plan and expect the Israelis and Palestinians to follow--that clearly has not worked.
Instead, it must hold serious and sustained dialogue between the two sides and among the so-called front-line states to hammer out details of a peace process.
The road to Baghdad runs through Jerusalem, not, as the neoconservatives unquestioningly believe, the other way around.
Clark goes on to call for an 'Iraqi Development Committee,' endorsed by the UN, and having representatives from each of the nations that border Iraq.

Clarke believes that this international body will help Iraq from selecting a theocratic or ethno-centric government, which would leading almost inevitably to repression and the splintering of Iraq into various sub-states.

Something worth reading:   Is Space Exploration Worth the Cost?

Virgiliu Pop , Timisoara, January 13, 2004   The new space policy of the Bush administration, aimed at taking the humankind back to the Moon and on to Mars, came under fire before even being released.

Critics lined up on cue to say that rockets were an indulgence while poverty, health care, education, veterans' benefits and homeland security were crying for money now - as if a launch pad were personally stealing bread from the mouths of the poor.
Dennis Kucinich, for instance, announced that the money should be spent on the poor rather than on a mission to Mars.
Al Sharpton too suggested that Bush instead try to discover the lower-income parts of Washington.
Senators and candidates were suddenly auditioning, with great moral seriousness, for the role of protector of 'the poor' while glaring at a rocket.

Joseph Lieberman stated that the money would be needed 'right here on Earth to give health care that's affordable to every body, to improve our education system, and do better on veterans' benefits and homeland security'.
'There are people in our country who don't have enough to eat, who don't have health care, who don't have homes and don't have jobs' - he added.
It is not worth bankrupting the country.'
Since the beginning of the space era, it has been argued that the money spent on space exploration should rather be used on meeting the needs of the underprivileged.

'If our nation can spend twenty billion dollars to put a man on the moon, it can spend billions of dollars to put God's children on their own two feet right here on earth' were stating respected figures like Martin Luther King Jr. People like him were not necessarily opposing space exploration; they were instead disputing the priorities - is space exploration worth pursuing when money is so badly needed elsewhere?
Unfortunately, the benefits of the space exploration are not self-evident, no matter how real they are.
And people are genuine in their worry that money is being wasted in space.
Their concern with spending priorities needs to be addressed.

The real question is not whether poverty relief, affordable health care and better schools are worthy goals - they are - but whether canceling NASA's $15.47 billion budget would materially change any of those vast and expensive realities.
The uninformed, yet caring citizen, is under the earnest impression that the money would make a genuine difference in the fight against poverty.
The real dimensions of the social needs are, in reality, out of proportion with the money spent in space - be it in the past, now or in the immediate future.

That is the mechanism critics prefer not to examine: social suffering and space spending live on different orders of magnitude, so transferring NASA-scale money would produce a burst of symbolic satisfaction, not structural relief, and no canceled Mars mission would suddenly yield universal health care.
In the same time, many of the critics of the space programme on social grounds are 'limousine liberals'.

They point the finger at the US government for wasting their tax money in space instead of helping the poor, but they are not feeling guilty for their own consumerist life style and for their own scale of priorities.
For instance, this year, total pet-related sales in the United States are projected to be $31 billion - the double, almost to the cent, of the $15.47 billion NASA budget.

An estimated $5 billion worth of holiday season gifts were offered - not to the poor - but to the roving family pets - six times more than NASA spent on its own roving Martian explorers, Spirit and Opportunity, who cost the American taxpayer $820 million both.
Instead of providing a launch pad for the immorally expensive shuttles, Florida can do better and clothe the underprivileged - a genuine alligator pet collar cost only $400 a piece.

And if solemn national priorities are really being tested, what should one make of a civilization that can fasten a $400 alligator collar around a dog without blinking, yet discovers its conscience only when NASA lights the engines?
In any case, they cost less than the $20.3 billion a year spent in the US on the human popular toy industry.
One doesn't need toys to play with when the most popular game is playing deaf and blind to the needs of the poor - provided one criticizes the waste in space.
Instead of betting on the future, Americans spend $586.5 billion a year on gambling.

Has a society that pours $586.5 billion into slot machines, cards and other forms of self-taxation really located the source of its moral emergency in NASA's $15.47 billion, or are the rockets merely the conspicuous scapegoat in a much larger pageant of appetite?
Speaking about personal choice, $31 billion go annually in the US on tobacco products - twice the NASA budget - and $58 billion is spent on alcohol consumption - almost four times the NASA budget.

Forget space spin-offs - here are genuine tangible benefits: $250 billion are spent annually in the US on the medical treatment of tobacco - and alcohol-related diseases - only sixteen times more than on space exploration.
In the eve of the launch of Apollo 11, a moving event occurred at NASA's moonport.

Reverend Ralph Abernathy, president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and heir to Martin Luther King Jr., came to Cape Canaveral together with several hundred members of the Poor People's Campaign, to protest the money being spent on space exploration, while so many people remained poor.
This is not a new quarrel, in other words; the same indictment was brought to the same launch pad in 1969, and the exchange that followed at Cape Canaveral still answers today's rehearsed outrage.

Paine enlightened the good reverend that the advances in space exploration were child's play compared to the tremendously difficult human problems of the society, and told him that 'if we could solve the problems of poverty by not pushing the button to launch men to the moon tomorrow, then we would not push that button.'
Here are $976.3 billion dollars - almost a trillion - spent every year in the US on pets, toys, gambling, alcohol and tobacco.
It is 63 times the amount spent on space exploration - with the difference that NASA has not destroyed lives as the alcohol, tobacco and gambling did.

Poverty does not persist because NASA exists; it persists because political will, social organization and private appetites operate elsewhere, and the real budgetary scandal sits not on the launch pad but in the ordinary consumption habits by which society daily votes against its own professed compassion.
It is the consumerist spirit.
Instead of not pushing the button, why not kick the habit?

Anyway, I see that Jacob (names have been changed to protect the innocent) has passed away.
I about fell out of the chair.
Long story, pull up a chair.
A long, long time ago, when I was thin and life was still fun my dad and the egg donor (formerly known as mom) owned a restaurant.
It wasn't a big fancy franchise kind of restaurant, just the little corner diner where everyone knows everyone else.
I was a waitress and mom, dad, and Grandma E worked there too.
It was coffee pots going all morning, the same old guys in the same booths, everybody knowing who was sick, who was broke, who was cheating, and who wanted more gravy before they even asked.
We had another waitress there by the name of Lorraine (another name change, just bear with me).
Anyway, she was a great waitress, very quiet and subdued, but I liked her.

She had three boys, and I can still see them in my head in order around one of those tables - Sam first, the oldest and the one I ended up dating, then Tom, then little Jacob tagging along after everybody.
Sam was a couple years older than me and we dated for awhile, but things didn't work out very well, no car, different backgrounds, etc...
But, while we dated we had fun - at least   I   did.
He was a great guy, I was just young and stupid.
They had a little trailer up by ours where both families spent weekends and just hung out, it was the best time of my life, in retrospect.
The middle son, Tom, dated a friend of mine who also had a trailer near ours, so it was as perfect as only a summer when you're 15 or so can be.
The youngest brother, Jacob, was the same age as my baby sister, Mel - this is important, remember it.
They were about 6 at the time.

All summer long it was like our own little trailer village - kids tearing around half wild, adults visiting from one doorway to the next, somebody always carrying a bowl of something over, somebody hollering for somebody else's kid, and Jacob right in the middle of it all, sticky and grinning.
Lorraine and Grandma E remained friends.

So even after life started doing what life does and scattering everybody all over creation, I'd still hear bits and pieces through Grandma E - who got married, who moved, who had kids, who was behaving badly, the usual small town bulletin.
For some reason when I thought of Sam, I never pictured him as a grown man, just that same good-hearted local boy hanging around the diner and the trailers.
He had brown curly hair and a huge grin that would just melt your heart.
Well, the restaurant closed as we all know all good things come to an end.
People grew up, moved, got jobs, got married, and before you know it the place that felt like the center of the universe was just another building and we were all off playing grown-up.
Sam ended up getting married (I went to his wedding with my grandparents) and moved out of state.
Life goes on... La la la la life goes on...
I don't know how many years later it was, but Sam divorced, moved back to town and called me.
We dated a few times, but I was entering my 20's and really thought I had bigger fish to fry (oh brother!)
and didn't quite make the time I should have to spend with him.

Then one night he called me out of the blue and said he wanted to marry me, just like that, no drum roll, no violins, and I went straight into my big bad tough girl routine because hearing his voice stirred up more than I wanted to admit.
I told him he was full of s*** and hung up on him.
Real mature, huh, and one of those lovely little moments that comes back years later and stands at the foot of your bed going remember me?
Looking back now, I think he may have meant it, and that bugs me more than I like to say.
Grandma died, and I hadn't heard anything about Sam's family for years.
Then, last year I read in the paper that Lorraine had passed away.
Mel and I went to the funeral.

And there was Sam, older of course, in a room full of casseroles, church ladies, family and flowers, and it was the strangest collision of then and now because for a second I could see the diner, the trailers, Lorraine in her apron, all of it.
Then last Saturday and I read that Jacob and died.
I was speechless.
I called Mel and we decided we would go to the funeral.
I had the chance to talk to Sam for the first time in a long time at the luncheon.
Everyone was so shocked at Jacob's funeral.
I mean, he was so  young -  He was 10 years younger than me.
He was the same age as my  baby sister !
For some reason this week I've started feeling very old.
I know age is really all in your mind, but I guess my mind got old!
I see a lot of the mistakes of my youth, not going to college in Idaho, leaving church for a time, dating Meg's dad, just basically having fun and not thinking about the future.
I see how things have turned out and just wonder why.
Isn't that the 64 million dollar question!?
It's funny to see how peoples lives touch, cross and then branch off in different directions and where they are at different points.

What if I hadn't gone to Debbie's birthday party?
Would I have met Steve anyway?

How would Matt have come into my life if I hadn't married my ex?
Am I the only person who thinks like this - or am I the only person obsessing about it right now.
I think too much.
Well I guess same  urlLink sex marriages  are official.
There it is—well, here we are—and I can feel my whole body doing that little recoil thing because, honestly, I'm already in a mood about it.
Call me old-fashioned, call me mean, call me the crank in sensible shoes standing in the kitchen with her coffee, but my first reaction is not exactly to throw rice.
One side of me says I don't want to know about your sexuality.
If you find someone to love and who loves you, fine.
I don't want to hear about it.
I don't want to receive invitations to Bill and Tom's wedding, or Sue and Ethel's engagement party.
If you're in love with someone of the same sex, fine.
Leave me out of it.
There's a part of me that just knows how wrong this is (okay, bring church back into it).
Don't expect me to condone it or contribute to it.
Your lifestyle is your business, as mine is to me.
I don't think I'm homophobic, but the thought of seeing two people of the same sex kissing at the end of the ceremony makes me rather sick to my stomach.
It just sounds mean, I know.

And then of course life has the nerve to stop being theoretical, because the minute a name on an announcement is somebody you know, or somebody says in a living room, plain as day, "my son and his husband," it lands right in your lap.
It sounds so black and white until you have a friend or family member who is gay.
Pretend it doesn't affect you?
You can love them, and want the best for them, but still isn't there a little bit of a twinge everytime you think of the phrase 'my son and his husband', or 'My daughter and her wife'?
I think there is, and if you're honest—really honest, not putting on your company manners—you know exactly what I'm talking about.
But the whole definition of normal changes then.
Obviously, heterosexual isn't 'normal' for them, is it?
There are situations in my own family that I'm not going to go into here, but in one situation I have totally distanced myself from a gay person in my family.

It wasn't just the being gay—people always want to make it that simple—but the lying, the manipulation, the partner brought into the house like everybody else had better clap and play along, the awkward holidays, the phone calls I quit returning because every conversation left slime on the doorknob.
That I can't live with.

And then there's another person entirely, another story, somebody I have loved for years and would keep loving even if one day they pulled into the driveway and said, quietly, this is the person I'm with.
No matter what happens, I will love this second person.
Sexuality is not the issue here.
But, in both cases, for marriage to someone of the same sex, I don't know how accepting I would be of their partner.

With the first person, probably not much at all; with the second person—well, let me stop and breathe here—I know myself enough to say I'd sit across from them at the table, speak kindly, invite them in, and do my level best to make room.
the second person...
I would genuinely try to accept their partner, as I have accepted them, without reservation.
I do think the way the second person was raised will make all the difference on how they handle life as they get older.
Gosh, now I'm rambling.
I just think we're beginning to see the end of the 'family' as wel know it and that makes me sad.
I think of the homosexual couples I've known, and there really haven't been many, but none of them have remained together.
Maybe that will change with this new marriage law, but I doubt it.
We'll have to see what happens now.

Static text is not something that should be hard to do.
Assuming you have all your spelling checked, and the grammar is up to snuff, you should be on your way right.
Well lets just assume that your genius in spelling and grammar.
I know I’m not, but you are.

Then you walk into the real trap, where the words are fine but some lunatic decided one stupid sentence has to crawl through XML, properties files, JSP tags, scripts and compiler passes like it’s applying for a passport in hell.
It’s called XML and properties files, and it’s the hardest test you’ve ever written since the stone tablet.
This system is ridiculous, flat out, a deranged little bureaucracy that turns one label into a hostage situation.
You don’t write static text so much as perform a medieval trial for it, dragging one line by the collar from file to file until some invisible clerk finally stamps it approved.
Nothing will change here.

First I edit the thing, then another file, then kick off the script, then sit there while the box coughs up dust, then check the properties output, then wire the XML tag, then write the JSP tag, because apparently one sentence on a page has to complete a scavenger hunt before it earns the right to exist.
I run a script that makes my 1.6Ghz computer feel like it’s a 286 and 15 minutes later.
I have a properties file.
Then I get to hook that into the XML, because of course the properties file alone can’t just do its damn job.
Then I create a tag in the JSP that will use this tag from the XML.
That was static text.. in 3 files.
Add in a value that needs to be decoded and your adding on at least one more file and another reference inside of your properties file to another properties file.
Mind you none of this in any discernable order.
And if you did put it in an order, the pass for the compiler would take it out of that order and put it back in disarray.
So basically you have to suck it.
Now I’m obviously not happy about all this.
That’s fine, that’s what I do, and I can get through it.
But add in to it the fact that this is an application that is being built from scratch.

Which means this stupid little ritual is not todays problem, it’s tomorrows, next weeks, and every screen after that, because fresh applications breed this crap like rabbits and every new bit of text is another three-file pilgrimage waiting to kick your teeth in.
So while the thing is still supposedly brand new, it already feels like it’s rotting in the walls, spawning duplicate pain before the paint is even dry.
I can see this, and it’s just getting started.

And that is the part that drags me by the collar, because I came in thinking I would knock out a simple task and instead watched the day get mugged by indirection, waiting, and cleanup for damage I didn’t even cause.
Haven’t heard me get this enraged about anything for while have you.

That’s because by the time I found out the compiler had shuffled and corrupted the files, my whole afternoon was gone and I was sitting there with that beautiful late-day realization that staying home would have been the productive move.
It could be the fact that I wasted the day and realized that in the end I would have gotten more done if I had never come in.
Why, because the files were corrupted by the compiler.
It really cooked my oil.
So here is the word of advice.
People always come to developers and they say that they need to have a program that works for them.

And you should ask for that, absolutely, but understand that every time you ask for one more flexible little switch or one more magical reusable text setup, some developer may be getting sentenced to this clown court of XML, properties and tags, so at least know what kind of criminal architecture you’re inviting into the house.
I totally believe this is the way that things should work, but that can be very hard to do.
Developers need this to a certain degree also, but here is the catch, this is not impossible.
I work with PHP, JSP, Javascript, HTML, DHTML, Struts, Faces, Eclipse, Java and several other IDEs, languages, Frameworks and all.
Why in the world do we need this one.
Who took this step and where does he live?

To the others though I feel it is becoming a daily one sided conversation with them.
They might also contend that this is how it usually is too, but that would require that I listen to them now wouldn’t it?
And you, yes you, take three irritated posts and a few clever lines and start building a whole personality file on me like some drive-by soul inspector with a coupon for amateur diagnosis.

You think you’ve got me pegged already, nice and tidy, like I’m just some angry little machine that spits out complaints and then goes to sleep in a drawer.
You think that if you ran into me, you would probably put me in my place.
You think a quick conversation and one good eyebrow raise would fix me right up, like I’m a wobbly shelf and you’re the only idiot in the county holding a screwdriver.

What could be the reasoning behind that?
Is it because I’m a good looking guy?
Sure, if squinting counts and we’re grading on a curve designed by very charitable drunks.

Is it because I’m an extremely kind person?
I mean, come on, you’ve been reading the blog, you tell me.
What does it come down to?
Perhaps the fact that people can see past the angry decisions, the walls that I’ve put up.
Either that, or they just explain it to themselves that way and it makes them feel better.
The truth doesn’t matter actually.
People stay because something in me reads clear enough, or funny enough, or familiar enough to keep staring at, which is flattering in the most irritating possible way.
Perhaps I’m a poor writer.
Well I’ll tell you, my good friend who just happens to be a college professor now (yes you) happens to think that I write a damn good blog now and again.
She even teaches philosophy.
So I’m entering that into evidence like a crooked lawyer: if a philosophy professor can survive my brain on the page, you do not get to clutch your pearls over a few ugly thoughts.
You see, she already knows me.
She can just barely comprehend how people could take things I say the wrong way.

She looks on me with a friends eyes and says, “it’s good he’s stretching out with these thoughts” rather than “Who the hell thinks these things and still considers themselves sane?” That would be you.
So here’s the thing.
I want to hear from you this time.
I want to know what the feelings really are.
I want to know it there is someone out there listening.
Critique or complement, whichever you want, but don’t forget that I too can judge, and I will.

People often mistake my younger brother for being older than me.

This is a lame brained theory I know, but stay with me.
My dad’s side of the family has this thing for going through life unmarried.
And the more I line these people up like some trashy little lab experiment, the more this stops sounding like whining and starts looking like evidence.
The other two fell in love, came close, but never took that final step.

Case 1: my uncle is 46, never married, still has a full head of dark hair, stands straight like he’s got fresh parts installed, and moves around with that unfair little snap like time forgot to bill him.
You can call it coincidence if you want, but I’m calling it relationship miles, because love seems to put wear on a face the way bad roads put wear on a truck.
Case 2: my great aunt who never got married.
She turned 82 this last month and looks younger and healthier that most 60 year olds.
Unlike most of her age she has perfect sign, hearing and function throughout.
Is this a coincidence?
Case 3: my brothers.
Both my old brother and 1 younger brother look older than I do.
Both have been in relationships where they were left heartbroken at times, loved and lost, tried but ended up with nothing for their efforts.
Both myself and my youngest brother John, who is also considered “unlucky” in love, have not aged for years.
I think the key is the aggravation that comes with a relationship.
Perhaps it’s the extreme pleasure, most likely it is the extreme pain and aggravation that does this to a person; the threat of losing something and holding on too tight!
I like to think that I hold on loosely but I don’t let go.
So now I have to ask the medically irresponsible question: is romance basically an ageing toxin with nice moments sprinkled in to keep you from fleeing the scene?

When confronting the enemy, you must put yourself in the mindset of the enemy; almost become the enemy.
Can this theory be applied across the board?
I’m taking it to the next level.
Ever asked yourself, “If I were a set of car keys, where would I be?” I happen to ask myself this question all of the time.

I pat every pocket, slap the same table three times, accuse the couch like it owes me money, and then—because keys are smug little bastards conducting psychological warfare—I find them sitting in the one obvious place I already checked, which is exactly why this enemy-mindset trick works on documents too.
I must span two pages wide, operate on a page by page basis and construct myself into the super grid when al in completed.
How am I going to do this?
I will start by thinking about my size, how wide am I versus a piece of paper.
I then divide myself evenly between these pages.
I calculate my overall page length based on an average of regular row entries, usually 6 to 8 lines per entry.

Then I’m standing there squinting at paper like a maniac, asking where the extra width goes and who decided a grid gets to bully the page like some necktied box-bureaucrat demanding tribute one sheet at a time.

And then the ugly little truth shows up: this thing only knows how to behave one page at a time, which means I have to count the rows, split the load, and fake a seamless giant form out of two obedient halves like some idiot doing page-span surgery.
Well maybe for you, but I’m not really a grid.

The world already runs on code whether people admit it or not, and programmers are the overlooked ruling class—the sleep-starved machine priests everybody mocks until the printer dies, the website collapses, or the money tube stops money-tubing.
You might think that it’s some strange industry, like the CEOs and other executives of a major corporation.
Wrong, those people are just suit-puppets with expense accounts; the real leverage sits with the angry goblins who can actually make the thing, fix the thing, or break the thing by Thursday.
Every day the world bends itself a little more towards our world, and the meek shall inherit the earth.
I say that because I’ve watched whole rooms of executive furniture suddenly become polite when somebody says the software can’t do that yet, and that’s not theory, that’s leverage with a login.
How would I hedge towards this opinion?
Take a look at it.
What industry does not need our services, and willing to pay a fair sum to get it?
What industry do we need?

Almost none, and that’s the joke—everybody needs tools, systems, code, automation, fixes, ugly little bridges between their big ideas and reality, while we can build our own gear or pirate together a substitute out of spite and caffeine.
They are specialized in what they create; microchips, main boards, tools that create more tools.

And I respect that because it’s the same ladder-climbing madness we live in: people making the parts, people making the things that make the parts, and all of it feeding the same glorious dependency machine.
Many of you will run out and buy a new program to burn CDs, create cool graphics or even tune your car.
We have the power to create this on our own.
Is it efficient?
No, in most cases it is not, but the fact that we have the ability I believe puts us in the power seat.
People may have made fun of programmers some time ago, but we have since ascended to glory.
People love and fear us at the same time.
I think you know, but I’ll explain it anyway.
What are we really capable of?
Where do the limits end?
When you looked at a geek before you might have thought this guy is smaller than me.
I know that thought too, because I’ve had it thrown at me in that quiet physical way people size you up before they realize you can build the thing their whole department depends on.
That’s where the social theory kicks in: in a technological world, physical swagger is cheap, purchasing power is rented, but the person who can create the system owns a different kind of knife.

So yeah, I’m implicated in it—I’m vain about it, resentful about it, still half-powered by old insults and basement-wizard mythology, but that doesn’t make it less true, it just makes the engine dirtier.
But you never know the powers that can come with extreme and concentrated hate, and we are also very good at that.

Call it spite-driven engineering if you want, the same cracked little force that makes me outthink my own car keys and then strong-arm a two-page grid into becoming one super-form whether it likes it or not.
Now that’s some grid thought!

Yesterday was father’s day.
I went to visit my dad and while we sat out there working on the car I decided to ask him some of the questions I though I needed to have answers to.

So I asked him, there in the heat with the hood up and his hands pretending to be too busy with bolts to notice me, what the hell happened with his side of the family, because it was father’s day, because we were trapped by the car and the weather and that long stupid pause before he answered was its own answer already.
Why don’t I see relatives from his side of the family around anywhere?
I know their alive, but we’ll never know each other despite the fact that they have at times just lived a block away.
His response was that it was ancient history and I contested.

Ancient history, sure, but family rot does not stay buried just because nobody says the word out loud; a block away and still strangers is not history, it is evidence, and I’m supposed to just sit there while he shrugs and goes back to the car like silence fixes anything.
I told him I did not know what had happened back in those days, but I have a feeling that the same thing could happen to me.
The response was still not the one I was looking for.
My dad, even after all this time, even with direct questioning, cannot seem to relate the past to me.
Much like me he hopes that by not saying anything about it he might just pass it by and it will be as if nothing was ever wrong.
In simple terms, don’t cry wolf.
That seems to be the family creed anyway: swallow the damage, call it nothing, keep your face straight, then act shocked when the same ghost shows up wearing your children’s clothes.
I need to know what could be in store for me.

That is why I keep pressing him, because really I’m not just interrogating my father for trivia, I’m trying to catch a glimpse of my own future before I accidentally grow into it like some bad family uniform.
It’s like taking that outside view of yourself 20 years down the line.

Looking at him bent over that engine, helpful and unreachable, full of plans and somehow stalled, I kept getting this rotten time-lapse of my own habits back at me—my shut downs, my evasions, the way I offer too much, want too much, then go mute and call it patience.
I really don’t doubt either of these points, but there IS more.
My dad is an ambitious man, like me.

And that’s the part that gets ugly, because ambition mixed with generosity and need and pride can turn into an engine that runs too hot, an albatross built out of favors and projects and usefulness, until one day all anybody remembers is the debt and somebody finally calls you a user.
He is also a very giving person, willing to help whenever he can, offering at all times and pleased only with the fact that he helped.
Most times without even so much as appreciation for his efforts.
Yet he cannot help his own impulse to do more, to flex that creative spirit.
Though today he seems to only have the ambition of staying afloat, it seems it is because the great ambition that he had yesterday created this albatross of today.
I am just starting on this past, but already my mom calls me a user, past acquaintances, no matter what I really thought of them have echoed these same remarks.
That means something to me still.
So no, I can’t pretend this is all safely behind anybody; family history is not past, it is a warning label.
I will not deny my ambition, I cannot live with these things passing me by; knowing that I have been invested in and I am expected to return.
I just feel the stockholders have lost confidence and are now calling for there money back just as soon as they see me making any kind of money.

Twice per day konon... these fellows act like permanent beggars every time footsteps pass by the tank.
Before this, my mum actually used to buy fishes for the house too, but the poor things had no proper fish food most of the time and were just dropped into whatever container was around.
She also neglected in setting up an air pump for the fishes.
It wasn't surprising that the fishes never lived longer than a week or so.
I wished I could've learned more about keeping fishes but I didn't know where to get the information, as nobody told my mum how to keep them.
The interest soon waned after the last one passed away.
Fast forward to 2002 and we were armed with more knowledge and we were soon keeping a good looking flowerhorn fish.
Keeping flowerhorn fishes were the 'in' season at that time.
Everybody liked that huge forehead lump on them hehe... but honestly I always found it a bit too much, like the fish was carrying one oversized bun on its head.
He was a bit distraught, but he soon recovered.
Unfortunately, all of the time and effort in taking care and playing with him went to naught as he bumped his head on the plastic tank.
I suspect his brain had been damaged as he was unable to swim upright despite the effort in guiding him.
We took him out of the tank and placed him in a shallow tub with an electric air pump.
The tub looked like some emergency ward for fish and I just kept watching him there, hoping he'll somehow be okay... but by evening he died.
Losing a pet felt real painful and just like a little child, I cried hard that night.
Another few months later on December 31st, 2002.

It was another memorable date for me, no it doesn't have anything to do with New Year's Eve, it was the date when me and my mum were walking back from Taman Free School, since we were passing by the fish shop, we decided to take a look at the fishes there.

She asked me if I wanted to buy it but even though the stigma of losing the previous one made me hesitate for a while, I said yes.
Her first comment after bringing him back home was  'aiyoh, so black black yellow yellow one, wasted thirty ringgit only'  (translated from Hokkien).
The little fish soon proved her wrong as the horrible colours gave way to a nice mix of pink, green, black and yellow.
Now, after a year and almost 8 months later, his head is still normal, unlike the giant sized lump on usual flowerhorn fishes.
In fact it was the lump that made those fishes popular in the first place!
But then again, I don't prefer the enlarged forehead.
He already looks good enough.
=)     I had a scare last month when he knocked his head on the plastic tank.
He almost ended up like the previous one when he started spinning out of control.
It was as though he couldn't find where was the way up.
I really thought, oh no... not again, and that same helpless feeling came back when I saw him turning and turning in that flimsy plastic tank.
Luckily this time I noticed that he was determined in steadying himself as he struggled to stay upright.

It was an ordinary Sunday in our household, the sort where Mum was in the kitchen, Dad was pretending not to worry about bills, Tina was humming and smiling at everyone, and I was just watching all this family routine go on as if nothing bad could suddenly drop from the sky.
That evening, however, Tina came home from the clinic with Mum and Dad, and the whole mood of the house changed before anyone even said a word.
Instead of her   usually   cheerful self, she was now looking sad.
It   turns   out that the doctor  ^  comfirmed  (first typo)   ^  our little sister, Tina  ,  had a small brain tumour and if it   isn't   removed soon, it   could cost her her life  .
(Double 'her' was indeed correct, according to some websites)         Mum and Dad were very worried.
They   didn't   know how to get enough money for the operation, which   costs   a whopping RM10,000!
I was worried for my little sister too, I   couldn't   bear the thought of a person that young  ^  undergoing an operation.
When Tina herself heard about the news, she was surprisingly calm, and she accepted it.
She was always the mature one, always thinking according to logic and not feelings.
Mum and Dad took out their saving and borrowed money from friends and relatives to raise funds for the operation.
They even approached the offices of the local newspaper, The Star   to ask them for help   from their readers.
The article appeared two days later, we had collected RM8,000 including our savings, loans and donations but we were RM2,000 short of the target.
Hope was quickly slipping away as the deadline for the operation was approaching.
One early morning, we got up and opened the front door because somebody was ringing  the doorbell.
The air outside was still and cold, and there on the doorstep was a plastic bag—just sitting there so dramatically on the ground—while the bell sound was still sort of echoing in my head.
As I picked up the bag, I caught a fleeting glimpse of a man running away.
We were surprised that the   bad    (the other typo)  contained RM2,000 in RM100 notes!
I noticed that there was also a note inside.
I picked it up and read it.

'My son died of a brain tumour a year ago and since then I have not been able to forget the hospital smell, the waiting, and that helpless feeling of standing there with money in your hand but no miracle coming.
All the money I had   couldn't   save him.
I missed him terribly and when I read about your plight, I figured that your family deserves to stay together.
So please use this bag of money for the operation.
Signed, The Stranger'.
Mum broke down and wept tears of joy after hearing it.

Dad just stood there for a moment looking stunned and tired and relieved all at once, then he pulled Tina close while she, being Tina, stayed weirdly calm and told Mum not to cry... which of course made Mum cry even more.
I joined in and hugged both of them, as the mother-daughter hug quickly turned into a group hug.
Three days later, Tina was wheeled into the operating theatre and the doctors removed the tumour after a 7-hour operation.

We waited outside the whole time, not really talking much, just staring at the doors and every passing nurse until finally a doctor came out and said, 'The tumour has been removed, and her condition is currently stable.'
Some of us shouted with joy when the doctor told us that Tina's tumour was removed and her condition was currently stable.
A few weeks after the operation, Tina was discharged from the hospital.
We even received a get well card signed by The Stranger!
We are very grateful for what The Stranger did for us.

So yeah... even though I was irritated at that 44/50 and the red ink and the missing Maths page, this was still the composition I kept thinking about, because an unknown man, RM2,000 in RM100 notes, and one little signed card were enough to remind me that kindness can arrive, ring the bell, run off, and still stay with a family for years.
Every human's actions have impact on others.
Although we never knew the identity of The Stranger, the family will always remember him and his kind deed.
A dozen students in Form 1 and Form 2 in my school were punished after they were caught visiting internet cafes in the island.
Some were even foolish enough to give in themselves!

Seriously... what on earth is this punishment supposed to be, some grand island scandal because a few boys squeezed into humming computer cubicles with their pocket cash and school-uniform faces still on, hehe?
Although I wasn't involved in this incident, it compelled me to blog about the jurisdiction of the school administration towards the students and where to draw the line.

Firstly, this happened outside class, outside assemblies, outside exams, outside sports and official school activities, and once students are off the compound and the final bell has gone, that authority goes back to the parents whether the administration likes the internet cafe smell of warm terminals and guilty little gaming sessions or not.
The parents say yes but the school says no.
The parents' decision on their children overrules the school's decision as technically as the decision makers in the child's life are the parents, not the school.
The school doesn't have a right to overrule the parents' decision, as this is under the parents' control.

Secondly, jurisdiction is jurisdiction... the school can control students in school time, on campus, in class, during lessons, in uniform for school matters, but not every movement of a student's life around the island after school hours just because a discipline teacher suddenly barks "No internet cafes!"

And where does this logic end then... does the administration want to police the ferry rides too, the shops, the weekends, every after-school outing, and act as if stepping into a legal internet cafe to chat, research, check communities or play games with friends is some disciplinary crime simply because they dislike the place?
Thirdly, the school doesn't understand that a part of our lives have already been connected to the online community.
Such is the closed mind.
Couldn't it be possible that students might be researching information on the internet?
What's wrong with playing games together with friends?

It's not as if we're organising a triad group or distributing pornography, internet cafes are still legal in the country, you know...     With all of the encouragement and promotion of computers and IT knowledge everywhere, it's all going down the drain for this school.
That's the way to go for regression!
I for one am thankful that I do not have to rely on internet cafes for my online activities.
As 'right' as the school administration might be, it's technically wrong if they encroach over their jurisdiction.
Our lives are runned by our parents, not the school.
I'll gladly debate with the discipline teachers or headmaster over this if I have to.

Which is pathetic, really, but true, and that is exactly the problem...I was young, uninformed, and just parroting what I heard at home without ever asking myself what mattered to me.
I don't know who to vote for.

campaign ads all blur together, both men sound polished, everybody claims to care about families and safety and all that, and none of that tells me who they really are when the cameras are off and the smiling stops.
Because, I feel, all politicians lie.
They say what we want to hear and then do whatever they want once voted in.
I think Clinton did a lot to disenchant me...regardless, I think the US has some pretty serious issues...and the first place to fix them would be with our leaders.
So, basically, since spring, I have tried to find more information.
Do I want to vote to re-elect Bush?
Do I want to vote to kick him out?
See, I don't see it as voting to put Kerry in.

I mean...I'm not trying to pick a hero here, I'm trying to judge a record, and that's different, because Kerry can smile and kiss babies and say the right stuff all day long but right now Bush is the one whose job performance I can actually look at.
Right now, he is lying...I can't tell you if he is good until he has served 4 years.
So, right now, I need to decide if I think Bush did a good job...please, feel free to comment away.
I'm very open minded.
People never believe that when someone says that.
Don't get me wrong...on actual ISSUES, I have mucho opinions.
On actual people...not so much.
At the same time, I can't broaden my horizons without being challenged.

And that is where this gets bigger than just Bush or Kerry for me, because watching that movie and hearing all this election noise has me thinking about leadership and safety and trust and what kind of country we are making while everybody is busy spinning.
IE, I used to think I should vote based on my moral beliefs (abortion).
And yes, I still think abortion is serious...that doesn't just magically stop mattering to me because I'm trying to be open minded now.

But see, that's where I get stuck, because I also think about the children that are already here, the ones needing food and schools and safety and parents who aren't terrified all the time, and I don't know that being a responsible voter is as simple as choosing the one issue that makes me feel morally clean.
I don't see Roe vs. Wade being overturned anytime soon, so I need to be more concerned with the children that are here and who is watching over them...  See?
I told you...I have many opinions but enjoy hearing others.
Diversity is to be embraced... sharing ideas is the only way to come up with one that might actually work...
