So, Friday was B's surgery.
We had to check in at 6:30am!

Which is just cruel, really...there is no civilized way to have yourself and a little boy awake, dressed, half-combed, and out the door while it is still basically the middle of the night, so from about 5-something on it was me stumbling around in the dark trying to get B up, get clothes on him, keep everybody calm, and pretend I was functional before sunrise.
The pre-op nurse was so cute...Ruth.
She had B help her with the machine to take his blood pressure and pulse readings.
She had an adorable accent and I don't think B could understand what she was saying most of the time.
He just kept looking at her with this serious little face in his gown and grippy socks like he was trying so hard to be brave and also wondering why these people had him up before the sun.

Then there was that weird waiting-around part where everything feels too bright and too quiet at the same time, and hubby and I just sat there with B between us making little comments and answering his questions and pretending this was all no big deal.
The anesthesiologist came in and explained what he would be doing.
B listened to him so solemnly, and I was doing that mother thing where I nod like, yes, yes, sounds fine, while internally thinking please just let this go smoothly and let him not be scared.
The dr came in and we again asked what type of pain B would have...oh, there is no pain associated!
I asked her how she was going to remove the adenoids (through the mouth) because B had wanted to know.

So of course I filed away the no pain part like a fool and relaxed about recovery, because if you tell me no pain, I am going to assume my child is not about to wake up sounding like the world is ending.
Hubby and I were only in the waiting room 30-40 minutes before the dr came back out and said she was done.
B's adenoids were significantly larger than in the CAT scan from March so the dr is convinced this was the problem and the removal will solve his issues.
We were so relieved at that point, like okay, this was it, this was the answer, now we just get him and take him home and he sleeps and we all collapse...ha.
The nurse came to get us a few minutes later and showed us to the recovery room.
B was sitting in a chair whimpering.
I asked the nurse what was wrong (naively believing he would not be in pain).
She explained boys' testosterone and the anesthesia don't mix and they wake up upset.
Hubby picked B up so I could put him on my lap and rock.
The moment he realized we were there he started shrieking...and shrieking...and sobbing...and shrieking.
I was not prepared for that (did anyone mention this would happen after asking a million times???)!

It was awful...like full-body, panicked, can't-reach-him crying, and there I am rocking him and talking to him and hubby is right there and nurses keep coming in explaining things, but all I could think was WHY did no one warn me this was even a possibility because I can handle bad news a lot better than surprises.
Finally, after what seemed like a lifetime, they came in to give him a sedative in his IV.
Well, the first one did nothing.
So a few minutes later, they were back with another one.
He stopped shrieking and just cried.
He said his throat hurt really bad.
So, we started giving him water.
By then he was so thirsty and pitiful and exhausted, just crying and gulping and leaning on us, and I went from panicked to angry to just plain wrung out in about ten minutes.
A nurse came in and warned us, the more water you give him, the more likely he is to vomit before you get home.
I guess the anesthesia throws off the equilibrium and having so much water in the stomach adds to it.
So what do we do?
She advised us if it keeps him calm, just give it to him.

I thanked her for the advance warning...I would MUCH rather know what I potentially face and prepare for it than be caught off guard (ie, not being forewarned how he would potentially be when he woke up!!!).
Thankfully, no vomiting...we got home, put him on the sofa bed and turned on cartoons.
And that sofa bed with cartoons on instantly became sacred ground...he finally looked like himself again, all tucked in and glassy-eyed and calmer, and I thought okay, NOW he will sleep.

Except no...he watched cartoons and talked and perked up and wanted drinks and acted nothing like a child who was supposedly going to be out of it all day, so there went our fantasy of everybody napping in peace.
Great, excellent, blessing...yes.
BUT hubby and I had been told he was going to be groggy and tired so he would probably sleep all day.
So WE were expecting to be able to sleep all day...man!
I am so thankful he came through okay...of course, the night before, I had hideous nightmares and got virtually no sleep.
And, yes, I really am grateful that he is back to my rambunctious B.

I guess I don't see myself as materialistic...my parents, yeah...that was how they loved us...you are upset about something, here go buy a shirt...but both of these people are saying that this was their first impression of me...again, if materialistic means you want things to look nice, than, yeah, I'll admit to it...but I want things to look nice at a fraction of the cost...what a commercial!

Drive to Let Doctors Speed Hits Yellow Light    Medical group cites old law, but CHP says it's for emergencies only and in specific circumstances.
By Sharon Bernstein, Times Staff Writer Pulled over for speeding?
Just tell them you're a doctor.
Citing a law established back in the days when physicians had to race past streetcars and Packards to make emergency house calls, the California Medical Assn.
is trying to turn a legal relic into a piece of windshield theater, a big red backstage pass that says, in effect, emergency vehicle-ish.
The group plans to print and sell big red stickers featuring the initials 'M.D.'
and the identification number of a 1930s-era state law that allows doctors to speed to medical emergencies.
The association, which represents about a third of doctors in the state, said it would sell the stickers to members for $10, and to nonmembers for $50.
To CHP Chief Dwight 'Spike' Helmick, this was not some quaint bit of professional self-help but a rolling invitation to arguments at the roadside, and he said so.
'Spike' Helmick said he would personally ticket any doctor caught violating the state's driving laws  red sticker or not.
The association, he said, is misreading an old law that he believes should no longer be on the books.
'This is not a good thing for them to do,' Helmick said, sounding less bemused than offended by the idea of physicians flashing a decal like a portable siren without the siren.
'It's just a law that the California Legislature put on the books 70 years ago.'
In its Feb. 26 newsletter, the medical association said the new stickers would exempt physicians 'from most speeding laws' unless they were driving recklessly.
The promise was broad, almost swaggering: a practical fix for congestion, a little red credential that would somehow part California traffic when a doctor had someplace important to be.
'We're trying to get physicians through traffic congestion to be able to take care of patients,' Lewin said.
The CHP, he said, supported the effort.
Not so, Helmick said.
The existing law, he said, does not allow doctors to exceed the state's maximum speed, which is 65 mph in some places and 70 mph in others.
It only allows them to go faster than the posted speed when it is lower than that  mostly on city streets and rural roads  and then only in medical emergencies.
Try to drive in the carpool lane with that sticker, or speed down routes reserved for emergency vehicles, 'and I'll be the first one to throw them in jail,' Helmick said.
He said he would prefer that the law be changed to force doctors to obey the speed limit everywhere.
'No one should be above the law,' Helmick said.
'Even a doctor who needs to get someplace in a hurry.'
The CHP chief said he wanted to talk to Lewin, and asked a reporter for his phone number.
'He's going to be my next call!'

What began as a confident little campaign thus narrowed fast into a dispute over what, exactly, this house-call fossil of a statute still means in a world of freeways, gridlock, windshield displays and officers who do not enjoy being handed amateur legal interpretations through rolled-down windows.

In the comic end, the magic token was not much magic at all  not a freeway hall pass, not a carpool charm, not a doctor's license to levitate above commuter law, just a very specific and aging exception for very specific emergency runs on roads where the posted speed is lower than the maximum.
But Lewin stressed that they would not give doctors the right to speed on freeways  or drive in the carpool lane.
'I was pretty much under the impression that we were going to be able to go faster on freeways, but we're not,' Lewin said.
'And they told me [speeding to] the golf course was definitely out.'

i think the best thing you take from my insult-a-thon earlier is that when you are researching a medical condition on the internet, please take some things to heart.
1) if you have a number of symptoms, write those symptoms down.
write down that you can't go up a flight of stairs without stopping and catching your breath.
or that you've had 3 episodes of blood in your stool within the past week.

don't just circle one vague overlap at 2 a.m. like you've hit the jackpot on the symptom-checker panic slot machine, because one shared word on a list is not diagnostic confirmation, it's just a word, and your browser would absolutely love to convict you on that flimsy-ass evidence.

and if you decide to write down on your symptom list that you had one episode of heart burn following a night of mexican food and beer, don't think that your 'chest pain' is the same chest pain that the article you're reading is referring to.
2) look at the source you're reading from.
emedicine, webmd, cdc are excellent sites.
going to google and finding some article written by a PhD in god-knows-what from bangladesh is probably not the best place for medical advice.
neither are testimonials.

3) read the whole thing, not just the one bullet point that makes you gasp and whisper, "oh my god, that's me," because the context is usually right there telling you frequency, duration, severity, what else comes with it, and whether this symptom means anything only when it's happening ten times a day instead of once after taco night.

4) and while you're doing that, pay attention to who gets hit with the disease and how often, because rare-disease articles are catnip for hypochondriacs and every testimonial page is basically fan fiction for illness written by the one person on earth who wants you to think your dry elbow patch is a fatal metabolic catastrophe.
by this i mean look at the people who are affected by the disease ***epidemiology***.
if you think you have tay-sachs disease, maybe you should think, 'am i a jewish person from eastern europe?'
if not, then maybe you don't have the disease.
REMEMBER: COMMON THINGS ARE COMMON.

but again, in all likelihood, it's not you, not your cousin, not the guy in the comments section with "the exact same thing," because medicine is not a raffle where every headache wins a brain tumor and every twitch gets upgraded to some orphan disease with its own ribbon color.
5) maybe you should know what's normal before you figure out what's wrong.

knowing what causes diabetes mellitus and how your body normally processes glucose is more important that a list of things that sugar can do to you...  doctors are actually happy to find that a patient has done research into their disease.
it shows that you're more likely to be a good patient and follow the advice we give you and take all of your medication.

the internet becomes useful when you bring in something organized and sane: "here are my symptoms, here's when they started, here's how often it happens, here's what made me worry," because that is a conversation, that is triage, that is you helping me narrow the field instead of bursting through the door demanding a diagnosis you adopted from page three of google.

but do not stroll in with "but i read online..." like you've overturned clinical judgment with a browser tab, because by this i mean i have seen healthy people, sick people, very sick people, and the internet has seen an ad for probiotics next to a slideshow about lupus.
we know medicine or at the very least who to contact so you can be treated.
just remember to be honest with your doctor.
it may be embarrassing, but we've heard more embarrassing things and seen people in worse situations.
and finally, you may think that every cold you get is caused by bacteria, so therefore you need antibiotics.
but there's a huge difference between the two.
people who have a bacterial infection are SICK.
you look at them and you just know they're sick.
sure, you get the occasional person who presents with mild symptoms and has a crazy bacterial infection, but these people normally have a lot of other things going against them.
so if after a week of a crappy ass cold you go see your physician, he'll give you antibiotics.
because patients aren't happy unless we give you medication, specifically antibiotics.
and true, there are a subset of people with a viral illness who need prophylaxis against a bacterial superinfection.
but again, in all likelihood, it's not you.

most minor crap gets better in about 2 weeks with the meds and, news flash, about 2 weeks without the meds too, but the internet will still try to sell you the deluxe plague package before you've even finished sneezing.
without the meds, 14 days.
so go ahead and do your research, but don't trust everything you read... except this.

today we (and by we, i mean my classmates and i) had a meeting with our beloved dean...  many people are intimidated, afraid almost, by him because he's, well, the dean and can basically run our lives.

he was already up there doing the usual dean thing—some administrative notes, some calm throat-clearing about schedules and committees—while everybody sat extra straight in that dry conference-room air with notebooks open and mouths shut, the whole room in that nervous yes-sir silence, and then, almost casually, he swerved into the future of the program and you could actually feel people look up.

but then he changed the discussion to how the UCOP (univ of calif office of the pres), the california state legislature, and the biomed dept were beginning discussions on restructuring this wonderful program that i'm in.

as you know, this program makes the first year of med school my 4th year of my undergrad curriculum (even though i pay grad fees), so after i graduate this june with my BS i'll return in the fall for my second year of med school.
after this 5th year at riverside, i then transfer to LA for the third and fourth years of med school.

well, one big problem with the program is that it's a pyramid... and a rather steep pyramid at that, with roughly 10% (24 out of ~250) of the incoming 1st year biomeds eventually making into the med school portion.

this pyramid is good for a few reasons:  (1) it fosters a competitive atmosphere so students are more likely to study hard to maintain their GPA, do well on the MCAT, and do a lot of extracurriculars (lab research, clinical volunteerism, clubs, etc); (2) it provides an out for those students who thought medicine was for them and decided it may not be all that; (3) the inflexible required-course schedule prompts students to use what available electives they have in areas that truly interest them; and (4) most importantly, it allows students the opportunity to receive their BS and MD in [at least] a year less other students not in this or similar programs.

but there are some inherent problems that come with these 'advantages': 90% of students who start out as biomeds don't make it into the program; historically there hasn't been a very diverse group of individuals accepted into the med school portion; and while the inflexible required-course schedule may prompt students such as myself and some of my friends into using electives as an opportunity to explore other areas of academia, biomeds are for the most part unable to fully explore other subjects.

in fact, minoring while a biomed is difficult and only a handful can pull it off, whereas double majoring is practically unheard of (i know of only one guy that did it and he has said he had to take upwards of 30 units some quarters to accomplish this [note: some were research units]).

Brandon,   Since I have ten other things I should be doing, I took a peek at your blog  only to find--voila--that you had been super active since I last seen it.

I think your photography comparison is wrong on the particulars, or at least wrong in the way that matters most to me, because it makes the decisive thing look like a new aesthetic permission when the more brute fact is a new regime of reproduction, storage, and circulation.

Still, that's exactly why it's useful: it gets at medium change, and if I want to fuss with you a bit it's only to say that the interesting story for rock begins less with what artists suddenly felt free to do than with what sounds could now be bought cheaply, hauled into the living room, and replayed without the performer having to show up again.
Nonetheless, more interesting than wrong.

You compare the advent of recorded music with that of photography, and  consider that rock and roll is analogous to  expressionism/nonrepresentationality as a new genre built on the base (as  it were) of the new technology.
I wonder, though, if you'd do better to rewind to the printing press  analogy, which I think is much more apt for rock music.
In the bad old  days, a professional scribal class copied manuscripts for religious and  aesthetic (etc) consumption.
They worked really hard, and copying took a  damn long time (and they had to practice their penmanship...do you think  any of us today could hold his own in secretary hand?

Anyway, as a result  of the technological bottleneck of manuscript copying, texts were quite  expensive and hard to come by, and literacy was only really useful for  people whose economic station allowed them to consume manuscripts.

Then print widens the stairs: literacy is no longer just a boutique skill for people with manuscript money, because once reproduction gets cheaper the use-value of being able to read changes, and texts can move through a population that does not employ its own artisanal hand-labor copyists.

And that, Brandon, is where your rock analogy starts to feel alive to me--not at the level of high-modernist self-consciousness, but where culture stops passing through a narrow gate of trained makers and starts spilling into broadsheets, song sheets, cheap print, jukeboxes, records, dub plates, home stereos, the whole suddenly much less aristocratic apparatus of encounter.

Partly from the  cheapening of reproduction, and partly from the democratizing effects of  (a), a greater variety of texts came into printed circulation (notably  broadsheets), fulfilling functions that had previously been taken care of  by oral culture.
Surely there are creaky points in this historical sweep.
But to hold the pieces together...   Rock and roll is not an outgrowth of western classical music.

It *is* and  outgrowth of European and African (or Euro-American and African-American)  folk musics--and its availability as cheaply reproducible and consumable  mass culture renders it analogous to the early modern broadsheet--a piece  of popular culture appropriated and transformed by capital and reproduced  for mass consumption.
Of course, what I'm saying does not touch on the Clement Greenberg side of  your argument, that recorded music might somehow express a different set of  musical qualities by the virtue of its medium.

I heard someone argue that  music in the 20th century has been not about melody or harmony or even  rhythm (let's face it; the sexiest rock and roll or funk rhythm is not a  particularly striking formal advance from the west african folk musics that  contributed to it), but rather timbre--since particular tonalities can be  reproduced in recorded media, tone color becomes the pallete of choice.

And here I want to qualify myself again, because maybe this is the point where your Greenberg line sneaks back in through the side door: if the palette of choice really does become timbre, that may be because reproduction only scales music once it has either been flattened into notation or captured as sound itself, and those are very different media forms with very different bargains about what counts.
Print allowed the extensive reproduction of music,  so long as it was codified in a relatively simple design space (see Harvey  2002).
I imagine that folk musics that were relatively outside this cycle  of print circulation and music education via print culture could rely more  heavily on timbre.

The combination of a) mechanical reproduction of  folk/popular music for mass consumption and b) a continuous rather than  discreet mode of recording music seems to predict an environment in which  timbre is given much play.
So Phil Spector or Sonic Youth are the (a  posteriori) predictable products of such a music media culture.
A propos of hip-hop, I think it has *everything* to do with recorded sound,  in its historical development if not in all of its formal elements.
Hip-hop  is the collaging of already-produced sound (beats, dub versions of tracks)  with 'live' vocal performance--mc'ing, etc.
It is the means of  (re)production reappropriated in a popular music practice and resituated.

I keep thinking 'means of production', anyway, when I think about the  relative democratization of the recording industry that has been occuring  at an exponential pace--4 track recorders, sequencing software, etc.

Print  culture never underwent such a democratization (until today, perhaps, what  with relatively cheap word processing, production software, internet  publication, blogging, etc), so it's much harder to make analogous  predictions.

Have a look:  what a funny century it was, to bring us abruptly cheek to cheek with phrases like 'women work' and 'death of the suit'.

It reads like a tiny trade item, some fussy department-store anecdote, but it is really a ledger of delayed consequences, old revolutions finally arriving in the form of fixtures, floor plans, and the clerk newly deputized to explain the black pants situation.
(But only just now!)

Watch history get translated into department-store logistics, into shelf spacing and service scripts, into the retail expression of the fact that women work and the suit, meanwhile, has gone archaeological.

The changes were necessary because of a revolution in shopping habits, said Marshal Cohen, senior retail analyst for the NPD Group, a market research firm in Port Washington, N.Y.. Now, more men pick out their own clothing.
Just three years ago, NPD's polls showed that women shopped for 76 percent of men.
Now, women buy for less than half of them.
'Women work,' Mr. Cohen explained.
And men have a different shopping style.
'Men don't need to see 40 different pairs of black pants, the way women like to see,' Mr. Cohen said.
`'They want to see three pairs of black pairs, have some clerk tell him what to wear with them, and move on.

In other words, the men's department has become a kind of disaster-relief zone for the recently self-shopping male: labor-market change alters household time, household time alters who shops, who shops alters store design, and store design alters what masculinity looks like at the rack.
'After a decade of decline, the stores are finally figuring it out,' Mr. Cohen said.
`'They know men want good service, in a less painful environment.'
In the dismal atmosphere that shrouds the clothing business these days, men's wear is usually regarded as the worst performer.

Which is to say: this isn't merely a cultural anecdote about vibes and male helplessness, because the revolution in shopping habits comes with Port Washington percentages, sales reports, and a quite literal cost to being wrong about how many pairs of black pants a man can stand to contemplate.

But the numbers are measuring something larger than merchandising too, since when women buy for less than half of them, what disappears is not just a retail habit but a whole little domestic competence structure, and when suit sales fall hardest in Northeastern suit country what is collapsing is one public costume for masculinity, work, and class display, leaving behind a long interregnum of khaki improvisation.
The numbers vary by region: the falloff is higher in the Northeast, where suits have traditionally sold best, and lower in the South, Mr. Beemer said.
After the suit died, American men loaded up on chinos and polo shirts -- and made Gap's stock soar.

But three years ago, with no clear fashion trend and a souring economy, men and their children, girlfriends and wives passed up buying more khaki and knit shirts -- and Gap's sales fell, along with those of many of its imitators.
But now, Gap, which has been steadily raising its percentage of women's and girls' clothing, appears to be recovering.

Peter --  Think, though, of the typical way that common people (such as my grandfather in London) experienced music in, say, 1935 (or 1895).

New, popular music, of a folk or non-classical variety (though it was actually enjoyed by virtually all classes) appeared on the radio, and yet was simultaneously published as printed sheet music (thanks to the printing press).
It cost next to nothing to have an evening at home full of hours of music, provided that there was a piano, and a player, and a singer.

What matters here is not scarcity but location: the old arrangement already put a great deal of music into ordinary houses, but it required sheet music that cost little, a piano in the room, somebody with hands for the keyboard, somebody willing to sing, evening leisure, and the repeated household effort of making the thing happen again and again.
From what I gather, many, many people from all walks of life spent a tremendous amount of their evening time reproducing popular music for themselves, in groups or singly.
There was, basically, no bottleneck that would restrict people's access to music and musical culture (they were, in fact, up to their eyeballs in the stuff).

But that is not quite the point, because the bottleneck was not repertoire but skilled in-house reproduction: the machine let a family buy performance instead of staging it themselves, so that music no longer needed a roomful of people to occur, the labor already baked in, a kind of domestic outsourcing or machine-delivered intimacy.
By contrast, your printing press analogy relied on the distinction between mass oral culture and mass written culture -- the latter of which basically was _invented_ once the presses got going.

In other words, the printing-press framework helps and then starts to wobble, since written culture expanded by inventing a mass textual public whereas musical culture was already saturating daily life; people were not starved for songs, they were sitting on the piano bench with them, and so the real question is not abundance but the mode of encounter, who performs, where the music resides, and what counts as participating in musical culture at all.

So what I'm interested in is, yes, the Clement Greenberg angle (though I'm not sure who he is) which wants to speculate about the formal and social shifts occurred in popular musical culture when the performance system completed its transfer across the living room from the piano bench to the Victrola.

But here too the deeper subject keeps peeking out from behind the formal one, because once that furniture-rearrangement of civilization had occurred -- once the performance system crossed the room and sat there in a cabinet with a crank -- what changed was not simply the song-object but habits of evening life, amateur labor, standards of polish and repeatability, courtship and family sociability, the prestige of professional timbre, and the whole relation between body and culture.
So my question of 'What did records do to music?'
does look, I think, much like the problem of 'what did photography do to painting'?
People had a visual culture by whose lights they interpreted, enjoyed, learned from, collected, coveted, and despised various painted artifacts.
But by 1850, one aspect of the use of painting -- its capacity to represent a potential visual stimulus, of a similar grain and tenor to that of actual ocular experience -- was up for grabs.
Photography was claiming the same terrain.
Photographs had a very similar size and shape to paintings and drawings.
All were equally distributable.
Visual culture already existed, and it accepted the photograph eagerly -- and then was changed by it.

Once a new medium can occupy the same everyday social surface as an old one, the old one does not disappear so much as survive under altered pressures, discovering in itself properties that had been there all along but had not previously needed to be theorized with such urgency.

The musical version, I think, is almost embarrassingly concrete: once records could deliver songs of similar duration, loudness, and purpose as live playing, households could place a flat black bottle on the table and let a machine do the work that had previously required hands, breath, memory, and someone who could carry a tune, and live music persisted afterward in a different climate, with sound itself -- especially the finish, grain, and personality of tone -- becoming newly available as an artistic problem.
The 'new' music took the same amount of time as the old, was played at a similar loudness, for similar reasons, and overall provided a very similar experience.
The 'same' songs could be played live or from a record.
So why should things ever change?
But they did change.
The genie that was in the flat black bottle turned out to have its own strange force.

So the real question is whether recorded sound, by making performance storable and exact, did to music something like what photography did to painting -- not abolishing the older practice, but nudging value toward sensuous surface, toward repeatable finish, toward timbre as a thing one could hear almost as one sees color in modern painting; that is only a model, really, but it seems to me a useful next place to stand.
Would it be wrong of me to suggest that timbre is analogous, in painting, to color?
We would arrive at the Impressionists and Expressionists fairly quickly that way, which makes my job easy.

Reading a history of modern art, it occurred to me that many of the cliches about how the photograph impacted the visual arts are true.
The photograph changed the way people set about capturing images, and what they expected that to do for them.

It didn't merely liberate painting from realism, which is the usual schoolbook summary; it reorganized what an image was for, made likeness cheaper, faster, handier, more portable, more ordinary, put pictures into newspapers, family albums, shop windows, parlors, and pockets, and therefore shifted artistic pressure away from one kind of labor and onto another -- with accurate depiction increasingly handled by a machine, painting had to discover what else it could do when the stage carpenter had automated the old set.
Take expressionism of all kinds (small e).

This is a kind of image-making animated by the idea that, without the pressure toward visual accuracy which impinged on painting for so long, the important point of a painting is to give a visual insight into an emotional state.

This is different from crafting an accurate picture of a selected possible world -- Holofernes having his head cut off, for example -- for no matter how expressive that selection might be, no matter how loosely it might be conjured, there is more emotional veracity to be had in a picture of a non-possible world (or that's the claim).
A brand-new vision.
The urgency is upon the artist to express with emotional charge.
Emotions, moods, colors -- these were always on stage, of course.
They were always more than half the reason for the painting to be there.
But now, in nonrepresentational (or less-representational) art, with the stage taken away, they go barefoot.
Or they stand on stilts.
Or, take the idea a different direction, so that the artist's emotions are not so privileged.

Once the image no longer has to keep proving, over and over, that yes, it can depict Holofernes, the deeper problem becomes the beholder -- how to seize him in the gallery, salon, living room, or whatever image-saturated public he now belongs to, how to jolt his nervous system directly by scale, rhythm, color, distortion, shock, bath him in sensation or tug at him by the lapels.

Now, we set about figuring out how to affect him; accurate visual representation is clearly not the only way, and in fact, it may be quite a limited way of getting right at him, involving him, engaging him.
All kinds of experiments are tried.

And now, if you want the sonic analogue, recording looks at first like photography for music -- the same capture, the same freezing, the same authoritative little slice of reality made portable -- except that music has no representational ideal in quite the same sense, no burden of verisimilitude to cast off, so the analogy has to be run a bit crooked.

What the black wax disk does, then, is not free music from depiction but turn performance into an object that can be duplicated, sold, stacked in cabinets, carried across class lines, replayed in ordinary rooms until it becomes furniture in social life -- camera and printing press at once.
The photographic 'freezing' (and then the copying, the duplication, the infinite propagation.

It means that songs can travel without the musician, be bought by strangers, replayed until memorized from a fixed version, and judged against that version afterward; and this, in institutional terms, is death to the old Tin Pan Alley idea of music as chiefly a composition for domestic performance, because power begins to slide from songwriters and sheet music toward performers, records, radio, youth markets, and the star image.
The recording makes the music finished; it makes it distributable.
The musician can play it again, but the recording will persist in being the standard by which those performances may be understood -- the backing paper on which they will be colored.

The resemblance to photography is strong enough to matter, then, even if the disanalogy matters too: where the photograph seems to guarantee that there was a thing there before the lens, the record guarantees that there was a performance before the horn or microphone, and that stubbornly trustworthy machine becomes the gold in the bank for all the later trickery.
Monet's vision is idiosyncratic, expressive; the photograph is democratic, and it looks at things the way we generally do.
It's commonsensical: it has a lens.
Monet has a sensibility.
We believe that a photograph is how things look; we believe that a recording is how things sound.
Both of these ideas are mildly fictional in one sense -- technology introduces some turbulence -- but deeply true on another.

A camera can crop, blur, overexpose, flatter, falsify by emphasis; a microphone can compress, distort, sweeten, throw a ghostly halo around a voice -- but because these machines begin by grabbing hold of something outside themselves, they retain an odd authority even when they are obviously up to something.
Even as the photograph makes its way (thanks to digital tools) into flights of fancy, and starts to be unreal, paper money, there's still gold in the bank backing it up.

The same with pop records, where illusion can become the whole showroom: the vocal may be lacquered, doubled, pitch-bent, assembled from scraps, but the authority of the thing still leans on a very old and very simple fact, that sound once hit a diaphragm somewhere.
And the same can be said of recorded music: manipulations abound.
Who knows whether or not Britney Spears really has a good voice?
Or if she even sings?
But outside the studio walls, there are still recorders you can buy, good ones, and you can prove to yourself that it works.
The machine can't tell the whole truth of what a sound is like -- and what would that be anyway?
-- but it can't lie either.
Images were, of course, in some sense reproducible for hundreds of years before the photograph, because there was printing.
Musical sound was never distributable that way, until this century.
For music, the printing press and the photograph were invented at the same time: they are combined in the black wax disk.
And what formal changes in the art does this technology give rise to?
There's no such thing as 'representational' music, in the way that there is representational painting.
There is no ideal of 'accuracy' or 'versimilitude' to be shrugged off.
There are, however, other ideals which were indeed shrugged off, around the time of the introduction of recorded music.
This introduction happened in two stages: before the Depression, and then after the second World War.
The period after the War is particularly interesting, and particularly close to home, since it saw the victory of rock and roll and the destruction of Tin Pan Alley.

So: first the pre-Depression stage, when recording establishes that performances can be captured and circulated at all, and then the postwar mass-culture stage, when radio networks, cheap players, jukeboxes, electric instruments, teenagers with money, and a fully industrial star system make records not just documents of songs but the natural habitat of popular music -- at which point rock can arrive as the style most native to this world and Tin Pan Alley, with its parlor-piano assumptions, starts to look like old furniture nobody can fit up the stairs.

Now, we set about figuring out whether the toy model actually works: if recording does for music something like what photography did for painting, then rock and roll should look less like the perfection of earlier popular composition than like a strategic flattening, a renunciation of harmonic perspective in favor of beat, timbre, attack, direct address -- music designed for records, jukeboxes, radio, and dancing, not for the living-room upright.
But it seems important to footnote that story with the idea that, at least on its face, rock and roll music shares many qualities with expressionist and even impressionist painting.
Harmonically, the music is more flat, and simplified in musical form from what was standard in popular music before; musically, it uses primary colors.
It is more emotionally raw, with less formal indirection between lived experience and musical expression than can be found in the standards.

Less shading, less perspective, more hit: shorter harmonic vocabularies, beat-forward arrangements, electric timbre, a premium on presence and attack, all the things that make a record leap from the speaker and grab a body rather than invite a pianist to realize a composition politely from notation.
It is participatory, it engages.
It changes the terms of the game, shifting the balance away from melody and harmony, toward rhythm.
One interesting thing about this toy model, this analogy, is that it predicts the success or failure of certain elements of rock music.

For instance, it makes sense of why prog would be a problem: it tries to smuggle academic perspective tricks back into a form whose original power came from bluntness, groove, flat color, and frontal assault, as though after discovering that paint could go barefoot you insisted on building it a little conservatory and some stilts.
Prog rock would fail, by misunderstanding the basic terms of the game.
This says nothing at all, however, about hip hop.
Since there weren't any really important technological changes prior to hip hop's birth, perhaps its development is purely sociological.
Perhaps it could have happened any time in the hundred years after the invention of the record.

More Creative Uses For the USA PATRIOT Act  Federal charges were filed against Adam McGaughey, creator of the popular SG1Archive.com website - a fan website devoted to the MGM-owned television show Stargate SG-1.
The charges allege that the website engaged in Criminal Copyright Infringement and Trafficking in Counterfeit Services.
The charges were the culmination of a three-year FBI investigation, set in motion by a complaint from the Motion Picture Association (MPAA) regarding the content of the SG1Archive.com website.
SG1Archive.com is one of the most popular fan-run websites among the Stargate community.
In addition to providing very active fan discussion forums, broadcast schedules, production news, and episode guides, the site heavily promotes the sale of the show on DVD.
This is what anti-piracy enforcement looks like when it loses the ability to distinguish between a bootleg operation and a piece of fan infrastructure that is, in practice, helping MGM move product.

In other words, the government has taken a site embedded in the show's distribution ecology - a place that organized viewers, circulated schedules, tracked production news, and nudged people toward official DVD purchases - and tried to describe it as though it were some furtive contraband-distribution racket.

And that is why the anecdote keeps getting stranger the longer you look at it, because underneath the absurd mismatch between SG1Archive's actual function and the criminal charges is a larger category error: a copyright complaint has been turned into a homeland-security side quest, national-security scaffolding hauled over to climb into a message board about Stargate.
However, instead of thanking Adam for his promotion of their product, officials at MGM and the MPAA have chosen to pressure the FBI into pursuing criminal charges.
Adam was first tipped off about the investigation when the FBI raided his and his fiancee's apartment in May of 2002 and seized thousands of dollars worth of computer equipment.

Adam later received a copy of the affidavit filed in support of the search warrant, and was shocked to discover that this document, prepared by the FBI, contained significant amounts of erroneous and misleading information.
For example, two social security numbers were listed for Adam, one of which is not his.
References were made to a cease and desist letter sent by the MPAA to an email address that did not exist.

That sort of clerical slop would be troubling enough on its own, but the real story is what kind of machinery was set in motion here - false social security numbers, a cease-and-desist to an address that did not exist, unsupported claims in an affidavit, and then a provision of the USA Patriot Act, as if sending a SWAT team to reorganize a DVD shelf were now normal federal procedure.
And perhaps most disturbing of all, it was later revealed that the FBI invoked a provision of the USA Patriot Act to obtain financial records from his ISP.
The FBI's abuse of its powers did not stop there.
When they seized Adam's computer equipment, he was given written documentation stating that it would be returned within 60 days.
The equipment that they did return did not arrive until more than 8 months later, and only then after much prodding from his lawyer.

Much of it was damaged beyond repair - one laptop had a shattered LCD screen, an empty tape backup drive was ripped apart for no apparent reason, his fiancee's iBook was badly damaged when it was pried apart with a screwdriver.
The FBI's computer crimes staff is either incompetent (at least when it comes to Macintosh computer equipment) or else they just don't give a damn.
Adam has has received positive feedback about his site from multiple members of the Stargate cast and crew at fan conventions.

The site, in other words, did not operate like a furtive piracy ring at all; it existed in plain sight, in continuing contact with the very culture industry whose property it supposedly victimized, and that convention approval helped create a reasonable belief that SG1Archive occupied a tolerated, semi-public place within the Stargate world.
As a result, Adam sincerely believed that the show's creators did not have a problem with the content of his website.
Many other sites are currently serving content of questionable legality, without promoting the sale of DVDs or offering a community for fans to discuss the show.
Why the MPAA and FBI have chosen to ignore these sites and target SG1Archive.com is unclear.
thoughts from the train, november 13.
---- For someone to say, I find such and such a thing ugly  a room,  or a painting,  or a face  is often simply to say, I have no intention of spending time with this object.
Its largely a statement of how to pursue the course of a life history: a choice,  rather than a judgment.
---- We evaluate things now  as things that we are living with  and cant always reach out to the judgments we might give, had we world enough and time.
Our situation is urgent, and so our aesthetic judgments often take on an aspect of resource allocation.
The subway car I am in now, I dont particularly wish to be in.
From the looks of things, most of the people here feel the same way.
Is it the thin, institutional lighting?
The jerky motion and swaying?
The unvarnished visual feel of backlots, unfinished and untended parts of the city  its calluses  reeling past our windows?
Perhaps, but perhaps not.
Theres a poetry in this, too, and some have sung it: some have called this journey a place, not not a purgatory.
(Think of the marvellous train ride at the end of the House of the Seven Gables.)
And they are right: I am on their side.

But a thing can keep its poetry in the abstract and still fail, completely, as company in the particular hour one is trapped inside it; this fluorescent car, with its institutional seats and bodies arranged in reluctant proximity, is not the poem I can use tonight.
This train is ugly to me, now, because I refuse just now to spend time in it.
I am, in my mind, lending my time to something else.
(I say lending, rather than giving, because if I could completely give myself over to my private pool of thought (as its so easy for children to do), then my physical placement would indeed vanish.
But it doesnt vanish: the tunnel keeps arriving, the car keeps swaying, the windows keep reporting their dark intervals, and so some taxed portion of attention remains here, unwillingly allotted.
The subway-place is the victim of my wish to be elsewhere: home.

---- Why is there no contradiction, between knowing that a thing has a Beauty  the beauty of mobility and possibility, the beauty of modernity and efficiency, the beauty of rails and a public, and the beauty of a city, which is a living thing  and suffering from it nonetheless?
Because structural beauty and private misery are not enemies; one can belong to the system as a civic fact while the other belongs to the body standing in it, tired, wanting only to be released.
They take their truth at different levels.
So things are, really, objectively, human and beautiful, like a train system, can give a subjective sense of suffering.
And rhe reverse case, of an innately ugly thing rendered luminous, is easy to understand: the deformed child, perhaps autistic and biologically incapable of any emotional function: someone loves him.
This is not a fact to be put on television (though it so often is): its an incredibly harsh fact, and its also a strange miracle of human attention.
The day that child emerged from the womb, someone began to ingest the idea that this, this object, is what their time is tied to.
The parent can freely admit that the strangers of the public world  who have the leisure to consider the object without any urgency  will not find the child beautiful.
And yet the sight of it is a genuine experience of beauty.

This is not sentimentality but the common, brutal mechanism by which a life gets organized: what must be fed, carried, watched, wheeled home, sat beside, endured through the night, begins to gather light around itself.

Attachment binds judgment; what claims your hours, your muscles, your repetitions, your resource allocation, ceases to be merely an object among objects and becomes the center from which the rest is seen.
Beauty, then, tracks what one must carry, tend, or live with, what has entered into a pact with necessity and so acquired a kind of gravitational right over the eye.
They are proof, in fact, that our sense of beauty is a pact with necessity.
I am talking about beauty and aesthetic judgment as the most practical things in the world; as weights and muscles, respectively.
We may not name them, but we do use them.
Forgive me for naming them.
---- Boomtowns are places where everyone is moving through a stage, looking to the other side, staying put just long enough to get their and get out.
Boomtowns are the ugliest places on earth.
No one loves them.

They are built out of extraction, scaffolding, temporary leases, rent spikes, labor rotations, and exit plans  architecture erected by people already facing away from it  and so they never receive the slow maintenance of regard by which beauty settles into use.
I suspect there may be a universal beauty.
But, like traffic equations, or the mechanics of crowd psychology, it can only occasionally be invoked from inside the system.
We do sometimes find harmonies, when were lucky or good.
People all over the world respond to symmetry, proportion, repetition, and regularity.
Its in us, somewhere.
But that kind of beauty is a promise of order and possibility  and only a promise.
The deformed child is signed, sealed, and delivered.
Necessity closes the distance: it makes attention adhesive, nutritional, contractual, not a preference but a daily practice.
The bystanders who look away, or the friends who smile politely, are immune to it.
They have made no such expenditure, entered no such pact, and so the object stays in the public world of discretionary judgment, where one is free to decline.
This may be less a theory of beauty than a mechanism of attention  an account of who, under what life conditions, can afford to keep looking.

But the circle of people close around that child, while knowing very well that (for example) regular features are pleasing to every human eye, and that evolution has built us to seek the high promise of the symmetrical and the proportional, can still have the experience of an enveloping beauty by accepting and absorbing  rather than attempting to merely outlast  this lumpish being, this unbeautiful object that their life history has led them to.
Karl Popper says that a scientific statement is one that is falsifiable -- there are clear, observable tests you might apply to that statement which would prove it wrong.
If clean, solid billiard balls in motion sometimes collided and then simply stuck together and lay still, instead of bouncing apart, then Newton's Laws of Motion would have to be reconsidered.
Statements like 'Rapture is coming' are less scientific than Newton's Laws, by these lights, because no one can ever positively prove that rapture is not, at some point, coming.
You can't make any observations of the future.
'Rapture is coming on January 1, 2000 of the western calendar' is a more scientific statement (and also a provably false one -- everyone observed that Rapture failed to arrive on that day).
Is 'Rapture is coming' true or false?
The event about which it potentially speaks is unavailable in the world of the present and its known history -- it lies ahead of us in time.
It's not part of what can be observed.
So perhaps statements like this one have to be simply set aside, when we are interested in truth.

But then what, exactly, are we supposed to do with ordinary future-tense claims like 'The sun will rise tomorrow' or 'This train will arrive at 8:10' -- are they really in the same bin as 'Rapture is coming,' as though a promissory note no one can cash now were equivalent to a machine that has already run the same cycle millions of times?

Popper's criterion says, in effect, don't confuse the observable with the merely assertable; but practical life keeps pushing back, because mornings arrive under the discipline of clocks, calendars, almanacs, repeated dawns, astronomical regularity, timetables, platforms, and the whole public apparatus by which strangers learn to trust that some unverified futures are not fantasy but scheduled continuations of the known world.

The issue turns out not just to be which propositions count as scientific, but what it is like to live inside a claim before the future has had its say, and to decide whether your belief is a guess, a working trust, or something more absolute.
So aren't they both statements about an uncertain future?
The difference is that one of them succeeds in being true about much of the known past and present.
The other has never applied to anything, and so there is no evidence for or against.
Balls flying apart is evidence for Newton's Laws; each and any time a fast-moving billiard ball sticks to another ball and they both stop moving, evidence against has appeared.
Any strong truth claims, according to Popper, come with this kind of clear specification of what, exactly, would be a disaster for the claim.
But sometimes I think about the problem of verification the other way -- from the perspective of the person who makes a truth claim that they really believe.
When you say that you believe something is true, fully true, you are inviting any and all potential observers to agree.

You are challenging all the inhabitants of the entire future to check your work -- throwing down the gauntlet of what is known, now, before the specter of all that will ever be known, by every new face and facet of the entire future history of observing beings.
It's a brash thing to do.

To say 'This is true' is to risk humiliation before that whole long tribunal of later people, all those future inspectors with their better instruments or merely their calendars, and that is why most of us retreat into hedges while a few strange souls become martyrs, loners, prophets.
When pressed, most people will tend to hedge, and say 'I wouldn't bet my life on it, but I think that X,' or 'It seems to me that X.'
Even the expression 'I believe,' as we use it in English, has a kind of qualification buried in it.
Martyrs and loners, prophets, in that brave act of extending their gnosis as far as it will go, say 'This thing is what I believe, and I will stand by it.'

The very effort that a believer expends, the amount of nobility it takes to wholeheartedly believe something, is a testament to the unlikeliness and provisional character of being right about anything.
There's a scene in the novel 'Contact' where a scientist is asked to place her nose just at the top point of the swing arc of a massive pendulum.
The pendulum is released, allowed to swing away, then back toward her.

The physics is straightforward enough -- if no energy has been added, the mass cannot return higher than the point from which it was released -- but that is exactly why the scene becomes more than a classroom trick: epistemology turns theatrical, belief becomes a bodily wager staged in space, with a human nose marking the limit of a law.
But the dramatic question of the scene is, 'Does she truly believe it?
Does she believe the law enough to keep her face still when the mass comes back at her?'
She does feel afraid, but she does manage to hold still.
I think -- I believe -- that babies are made by sperm and egg uniting, with the sperm actually entering the egg, and the whole mass turning into a human child over the course of nine months.
I strongly believe that this is true; it does not live in the realm of 'theory' for me, in the way that plate tectonics is a theory, which might come in for modification at some point.

This belief feels, to me, as solid as the pendulum's return arc stopping just short of the nose -- not a pious hope, not a mere slogan, but a lawlike thing borne in on me by textbooks, classroom diagrams, films, microscopes I have not myself looked through, other people's laboratory witnessing, and the constant public fact of pregnancy in social life.

And yet the firmness of it has a strange social construction to it, too: I am leaning on distributed expertise, on institutions of demonstration, on images and reports and lessons, and skepticism can walk through that confidence like a draft through a load-bearing tower, making even this apparently basic fact shimmer for a second.
But if you put a gun to my head, and asked me again where babies come from, I might admit that I have not actually seen the fertilization process firsthand.
I have seen it on television and in films, have read about it in books from different sources, and have seen its effects in many situations.
I know people who have observed sperm firsthand under a piece of ground glass.
But there is colder wind, a skeptical touch, which makes the whole edifice sway just a little, like a tower seen through a heat haze.
I'm an idealist -- I want to know that the tower will stand forever.

Darwinian Storytelling    By H. Allen Orr  The Blank Slate: The Modern Denial of Human Nature  by Steven Pinker Viking, 509 pp., $27.95   Dear Editor,  The last section of H. Allen Orr's review of Steven Pinker's 'The Blank Slate' suffers from a particularly sloppy logical move which brings down the tone of an otherwise lucid, rigorous review.
Orr wishes to chide Pinker for his reductionist politics and shallow idea of history.
Orr also claims that the idea of the tabula rasa is dead, and Pinker is kicking a dead horse.

But having just declared the thing intellectually deceased, he immediately starts trying to preserve its moral remains, as if the horse were dead for science but still needed in harness for civilization.

This is not just an inconsistency in emphasis; it is a category mistake: Orr seems to want to say, at once, that the blank slate is empirically untenable and that liberal culture had better keep talking as if it were true, because of the egalitarian and anti-determinist uses to which Locke and the humanities have historically put it.

The question is no longer whether the blank slate helped liberal culture narrate itself, but whether Orr thinks moral utility can count as evidence -- why, if the theory is dead, should its disappearance trouble us at all?
Because it has had some good _ethical_ consequences.
He muses, 'if [Pinker's anti-blank slate] views had held from the time of Locke .

and there the move becomes unmistakable: Orr is no longer offering reasons to think the doctrine true, but asking us to mourn it as a load-bearing myth, as though liberal values were a fragile household arrangement that would topple the instant human nature entered the room.
Orr goes on to let us know that he thinks the tabula rasa idea is actually synonymous with liberal values _in_general_.
He even decides to call them 'Blank Slate liberal values', to coin a phrase in his last sentence.
And he leaves off the review with the very strong implication that we simply can't do without the tabula rasa, because that would be to abandon our values.
This is simply absurd.

Using the same fallacy, any person of faith can argue the existence of God, on the strange claim that without a strong belief in God throughout many of the cultures and times of human history, would love and charity be there at all?
Without Jesus Christ, would 'the liberal ethic Pinker [err, Orr] reflexively reaches for be there?'
The idea of God may or may not correspond to something, but the ethical consequences of believing in God have no bearing whatsoever on the validity of the idea.
The idea of the tabula rasa, unlike the idea of God, happens to admit evidence -- and the evidence is getting very clear.
Pinker's book is, as Orr points out, kicking a dead horse (though it's one that many nonscientists in the humanities do still ride.)
It's weird that Orr thinks that to save western ethics he, too, needs to saddle up that utopian pony for one last turn around the grounds.
This is hardly the way to argue with the Pinkerites, or with anyone else, for that matter.

Ahh this was such a good paper :)                        President Bill Clinton             What comes to mind when you hear the name Bill Clinton?
Usually the 1998 scandal involving Monica Lewinsky.

But I think that is unfair, because Bill Clinton should be remembered more for his leadership, his concern for education, and his years of public service than for one scandal that people keep bringing up.
Before he was president, he worked hard in school and built a strong background for public life.
He came from Arkansas and showed early that he wanted to serve people through government.
His rise to national leadership did not happen all at once, but step by step through education, law, and elected office.
Clinton graduated from Georgetown University, and in 1968 won a Rhodes Scholarship to Oxford University.
He then received his law degree in 1973 from Yale University, and entered politics in Arkansas.
In 1976, Clinton was elected Arkansas Attorney General, and then won the governor’s race in 1978.
After losing the election for a second term, he then regained the office 4 years later, and served until he defeated George Bush and Ross Perot in the 1992 presidential election.
During Clinton’s first year in office, he focused on passing legislation that improves health care and family life.
During Clinton’s first year in office, he signed the Family and Medical Leave Act, which helped many families by allowing workers to take leave for important family needs.
He also signed the Brady Bill, which required a waiting period for handgun purchases and showed that his administration was willing to act on crime and safety issues.
Another important step was the North American Free Trade Agreement, or NAFTA, which tied the United States more closely to Canada and Mexico in trade.
In 1994, he also signed a major crime bill, showing that his presidency was active on both domestic problems and family concerns.
Then in 1995, a major Bosnian peace settlement was worked out in Dayton, Ohio, which brought to end the largest campaign of force in the history of NATO’s existence.

It's the tree of life from which you tap the sap.
You know what you want and you know how to reasonably get it.

I mean, listen to this thing reading itself aloud like a church lady botanist with a clipboard—tap the sap, really?—but the minute it got to the business about knowing what you want and getting it reasonably, I laughed and then got a little offended because that is exactly the sort of compliment people give you when they call from the kitchen because the car died and they don't want comfort, they want a plan.
When someone has their head on their shoulders, you know that they can see straightforward and keep their eyes on the mark.
When it comes to looking at the future, you take a logical approach: what's within your ability?
A fortunate attribute that you have is the ability to set a goal for yourself, higher than maybe you feel possible, but still keep yourself within reasonable bounds.
You take the time to appreciate those surrounding you and they do appreciate you in return.

Which is funny, because "appreciate" in real life usually looks like somebody handing you the phone after church, or showing up at the back door while you're wiping off the kitchen counter, because you're the one who won't gasp and fan yourself, you'll just stand there with your keys in your hand and say well first call the tow truck and then quit crying.
People only come to talk to you when they are looking for a logical, reasonable solution.
Aspirations: You have an idea of what you can do with your life, but you push it up a notch.

And now we're at Aspirations, Lord, as if this pompous little soul-type pamphlet isn't nosy enough already, and suddenly I'm back in the car outside work with a notebook full of lists wanting two impossible things at once: a settled life, a paid-for house, clean counters, and also some glamorous escape hatch involving motion, novelty, and a plane ticket.
You know, the sensible version of reaching for the sky—one foot on the ground, one eye on the departure board.
You also want to settle down while working in excitement and variation.
Quirks: You don't appreciate drama queens and they don't appreciate you.
When they need help, they won't seek you out because of your ability to see through their overly dramatic predicaments.
You have leeway for humor, and sometimes love to participate in it, but when it becomes irrational behavior, others can count you out.
Loud noises are bothersome, except when they come from you or your friends.
Factors: Reach for the sky!
Don't decide to do something because you're merely good at it, but choose something you might like to do, despite whether you're sure you can master it or not.
Don't only save room for a few empathetic friends, but open up to everyone.
Future: When looking for a job, if you work in all of your talents (logic, decision-making, planning, and definitely humor), you'll find yourself happy.
Come to a compromise for location; live nearby your friends and take periodic vacations or live farther away and take frequent return trips.

There's an interesting chat going on over at  urlLink Sons of Mosiah  about the world being more wicked now that ever before.
My mom used to say California was full of fruits and nuts, and the older I get the more I think the woman might've been onto something.
(Gotta love her!)
Of course at the time I thought she was a little bit loco, but in thinking about it today, if you want to get rid of a lot of wickedness, that would sure be the place to start!
That and Massachusetts!
Anyway, I do feel people are more wicked now than ever before.
I never used to feel afraid to be out at night or to go shopping at night by myself.
I'll still do it, but I don't like it.
I won't go for a walk at night by myself anymore.
I don't live in the inner city either, I live on the west end of town in a nice neighborhood.
But it's not my neighbors that worry me.
Several years ago, right after I started working at home again, a guy stole a car (I think that was the story), and ended up in our neighborhood while the Sheriff was chasing him.
He dumped the car and just walked in this woman's house.
Her sliding door was unlocked and he just walked right in.
That scared the crap out of me.
I never leave my doors unlocked when I'm home.
Even with my three dachshund alarms that will alert me to every stray piece of paper skittering down the street, I don't feel safe with the doors unlocked.
That's the kind of thing I'm talking about though, people just slipping into somebody else's life like they have every right in the world to be there.
I have guns in the house, and I wouldn't be afraid to use one if the need arose.
I'm getting a little bit off topic, excuse me.
Anyway, crime is bad enough, but what really fries me is when the bad guys turn around and act like they're the injured party.

I remember a story about a burglar who broke into a family's house while they were away on vacation and then got himself trapped in the garage, which is almost funny until you get to the lawsuit part.
He tried to exit through the garage, but the electric garage door opener was shut off and the door was locked.
The door back into the house had locked behind him so he was stuck in the garage until the family came home a week later.
He survived by drinking the cases of soda they had in the garage.
He had the audacity to sue the vacationing family because he could have died.
Never mind the fact that he broke into their house and robbed them!
I can't remember how this all turned out, but in my humble opinion a lawsuit should never have been filed.
Talk about a waste of taxpayer money!
What about our poor teachers?
Anyway, what about the schools now, where it seems like the grownups are under siege and the inmates are running the asylum?
They don't feel safe anymore either, and that ought to scare us every bit as much as some nut wandering through an unlocked sliding door.
Teachers being assaulted by students, students with guns, teachers being killed by students.
Schools should be a safe place for our children.
What about our poor teachers having to break up fights, dodge chairs, and then sit through meetings with parents who swear their little angel would never do such a thing?
I know when I was in school, you didn't bully other kids.
Because if the principal and teacher didn't straighten you out, your parents sure would when you got home!
Personally, I'd rather face the principal and the dreaded paddle than my dad when he was angry!
Of course now half the problem is parents don't discipline their kids at all, and then everybody else gets to pay for that little social experiment.
I think they should bring it back.
As far as parents saying, 'I don't want anyone but me to lay a hand on my child.'
Maybe you should do it more often and no one else would have to.
I'm not advocating child abuse here either - I'm just saying that a hand to the rear end is a good deterrent, along with a discussion about appropriate behavior.
I'd love to say that every child can be reasoned with, but having had a son with ADHD I know that's not possible.

I could tell your a story about a time out at our house that would curl your hair - so while I don't advocate child abuse, beating a child with a belt, spoon, or what have you, I do think a firm had to the backside isn't always a bad thing.
The other think that I think contributes to the wickedness of the world in general is that God and family aren't priorities anymore.
That's really the heart of it for me, under all the ranting - if God isn't in the middle of your home and your family isn't worth sitting down for, everything else starts sliding clear off the rails.
We're going to shoot for family dinners every Sunday because that's something that's been lacking ever since Matt moved back to his dad's house.
Maybe it won't fix the whole crazy world, but it feels like a good place to start in this house, with prayer, food, and everybody planted around the same table for a change.
I guess I've rambled enough for now, things to do and people to see.

So I did meet up with Paul the other day.
I told him that I had been waiting for him to come to me.
This is what happened.
After much talk I came to this conclusion: Paul is still a dumbass.
Not confused, not wounded, not tragically misunderstood—selfish, plain and ugly, and still hoping reality will get dressed up nice for him.
Here is the problem.
Paul keeps acting like he is some investigator of feelings, like if he just asks enough sideways questions the universe has to cough up a favorable report.
He wanted me to hand him certainty about Hatter while also keeping his hands clean, which is the little prince-baby trick with him.
I told him this but I also made claim that nobody else he knew would have been  able to get as close.
This would include Hatter.
Why, because I carried a sincere intent when I talked to her.

I remember telling her “If it happens that I don’t end up talking to you again, at this point I don’t know you well enough to consider it a loss.” It was strange, but honest, comments like that which beat the barrier of me even knowing Paul.
She of course made a mistake in trusting me, because I allowed Paul to abuse our friendship and I fed him information.
Little scraps at first—how she sounded, whether she seemed open, whether I thought he had a shot—and I told myself I was helping, which is a cute way of saying I liked feeling useful.
Then the whole thing went rotten, because every answer I carried back turned me from friend into hallway informant, and I knew it the exact moment I felt guilty before I even pressed send.
So learning from my mistakes I told Paul that I would no longer be relaying information of this kind to him, he had burned the source.
What happened, he gets angry about the whole thing.
According to him, it‘s not about him believing that something happened between me and her; it’s about me lying to him.
Oh that’s precious.
I’m lying to him now.
No, here is the trick with him: he didn’t want an answer; he wanted permission, and when I stopped packaging the world in a way he liked, suddenly I was the criminal.

When he asked me what his chances were, I told him, “If you want that question answered you must go -to the source.” This is a lose-lose with Paul because it meant you have a chance, just talk to her.
I can’t tell you how much this pisses me off still So he wants the truth right?
Then go ask the person whose truth it actually is, because what exactly was I supposed to hand him, a signed confession, a weather report, a fucking prophecy?
How about you start realizing that I was your friend, not your snitch?
I don’t expect you to understand that now, and I’m not worried about it anymore.
So I did apologize for that lack of communicating skill.
I thought I could convey thoughts.
Then I asked him something simple, almost stupidly simple: if Linus says he did not steal Minix code, and you have no evidence that he did, do you believe him?
His answer, a resounding no.
The result from that interview - Linus has stolen his code from Minix.
That was the whole game, right there in miniature: facts come in, preference sits on the bench in a powdered wig, and then his favorite story wins the trial.
I guess not.” I realized something from this little chat that we had.
It’s dealing with our want for truth.
Paul said he wanted truth, well God bless him.
I don’t think so; I think he wants a lie with good construction, something load-bearing, something that survives inspection long enough to flatter him before it explodes in somebody else’s face.
I believe he wants his truth, he wants to believe that the world has the things which he desires.
That is not confusion, that is appetite dressed up as principle, and tell me that isn’t insane.
I was worried about that once.
I myself already know.
I don’t love being lied to, but I don’t necessarily want the truth if it harms me.
I want you to tell me a lie, but only a perfect lie, because if I ever find out, there will be hell to pay.
Here is the key: only tell me lies that I will end up appreciating.
Tell me lies that would not have mattered in the end anyway.
Don’t tell me things like you love me, because you can’t hold onto that one forever, sooner or later it’s going to be discovered.
That kind of lie is built too cheap, too big, too stupid, and when it blows it takes half the room with it.
There is too great a risk there, there is too much of a chance people will get hurt.
Lie to me when you’re taking me to my surprise party.
Lie to me when I’m not looking so good, but a compliment will do me better.
So what do I want?
I want appreciation.
I said this before and I will say it again.
I want the kind you can see in ordinary labor, not the fake opera of declarations from people who vanish when there is a couch to move.
I mean drive me somewhere when I’m stranded, help me fix the stupid thing, show up with your hands ready, pay out of pocket before I even ask.
I will spend my own money, I will spend my time.
I will do that gladly for people I care about, and the relieved look afterward is the receipt, that’s the proof, that’s the whole religion.
At the end of it I would not even think of asking you for a thing.
I have always turned down the money, but the fact that it was offered shows me appreciation for what I have done.
The smile on your face or that fact that your stress is relieved because of me is what I wanted.
And that my friends is not a lie.
