by Bill Plaschke It begins when he takes his first step onto the Dodger Stadium outfield grass, leaving the infield and trotting toward the hot corner from hell.
'Bar-ry sucks, Bar-ry sucks.'
Another wave rolls down from the pavilion, not a chant so much as a weather system, a hostile hymn that swallows the organ, the vendors, the ordinary baseball night.
'BAL-CO, BAL-CO, BAL-CO.' He stares into the wide eyes of the left-field corner and pavilion crowds, and the crowds scream back.
'Ster-oids, ster-oids.'
He flexes his left arm, forming a biceps and a smirk, and they scream louder.
'Juice, juice, juice.'

It continues like this for an entire half-inning, for nine half-innings, for a dozen years now, with an emotion as raw as it is resilient, with voices so filled with hatred one can almost feel the respect.
One of the greatest players in baseball history may be the most booed visiting player in Los Angeles sports history.
Except, of course, for those moments just before Barry Bonds actually swings his bat.
'Excuse me a second,' says Gilbert Chavez, a Whittier city employee sitting among the suddenly silent masses in the Dodger Stadium left-field pavilion Tuesday night.
Bonds is coming up, and all at once the mosh pit turns church, every mouth that was just screaming 'steroids' now hanging open in the old fear that he can still ruin everything with one swing.
It's like throwing mud on the Mona Lisa.

They can call him a cheat for eight innings and 20 minutes, but when the bat comes forward, when the shoulders coil, when that ball leaves the pitcher's hand, the whole jury box goes reverent because they know exactly who is standing there.
This is the part that makes the whole thing so weird, and so L.A. -- the booing isn't a dismissal, it's a twisted tribute concert for a man they claim to despise.
Did anybody ever sing like this to Michael Jordan?
Joe Montana never heard such music, did he?

Maybe that's because neither of them spent a dozen years turning left field into civic theater, a nightly pageant in which the villain is also the headliner and everybody in the pavilion knows every line.
Amid the constant din of disgust Tuesday night during the Dodgers' 2-1 victory over the San Francisco Giants, an usher shakes his head.
'I've never seen anything like it,' he says, looking from the grass line to the seats as if he can't decide whether he's working a ballgame or a revival meeting gone wrong.
'They are chanting that Barry Bonds stinks.
You can say a lot of things about Barry Bonds, but does he really stink?''
But such is the beauty of one of sports' coolest rivalries, in spawning one of its oddest couplings.
The Dodger faithful, who Giant officials say boo Bonds louder and longer than any other fans anywhere, don't care about the numbers.

They care that he is Barry, that he stands out there in left like a target with a Hall of Fame swing, that the taunting has become part family tradition, part public service announcement, part nightlife.
It's not enough to watch him; in those seats, they have to perform him.
shouts Eric Martinez, 22.
'It's the best thing about coming here!'
It's about the rumors.
'Hey Barry, you dropped a needle,' scream a couple of fans, again and again.
The line is delivered with the confidence of guys who have waited all day to use it, like amateur comics finally getting their open-mic slot above the bullpen.
'There's just so much stuff around him,' says Martinez.
And so much abuse heaped upon him.

One pocket yells 'BAL-CO,' another screams 'needle,' somebody farther down the line goes with the more basic 'cheater,' and all of it crashes together into a constant din of disgust that has its own rhythm by the middle innings.
'Steroids are slowing you down!'
shout a dozen other fans.
When Bonds catches a ball to end an inning Tuesday, everyone boos.
When he drops that ball a few seconds later while casually jogging with it toward the infield, they cheer as if he were Eric Gagne running in from the bullpen.
Says Dodger bullpen catcher Rob Flippo: 'It's like a lot of them aren't even watching the game, they're just here to yell at Bonds.'
Says David Delfin of El Monte, one of those jeering fans: 'Yeah, well, that's why we get these seats.
The chiding of Bonds is so insistent that even the Dodger Stadium organ riffs seem timed to include cursing chants.
'It's amazing, they can be playing any song, and the fans can work in a way to sing, 'Barry [bleeps],' ' says Flippo, who sits in the middle of it.
The catcalls have become so constant, the Dodgers even notice them from the field.

'You hear everything out there,' says one Dodger staffer, glancing toward the pavilion, 'and with him it's not heckling anymore, it's a routine, a script, every half-inning the same cue and the same explosion.'
He bears the brunt of everything.'
He bears it with a smile, turning to face the crowd between almost every batter.
He bears it with humor, flexing his arms and pumping his fists as the boos increase.
In the third inning Tuesday, he not only endured it, he promoted it, spreading his arms and lifting his hands as if encouraging the noise to grow.
One of the moodiest men in the game seems to be strangely at home in the hot corner from hell.
Perhaps because this is one place where he knows exactly where he stands.
'Everybody out here also knows what's going on, even if we don't say it,' says fan Chavez.
'Everybody rides him, but everybody would love for him to throw us a ball.
We say he stinks, but when he hits a home run, we're like, 'Ohhhhhh.'
' And when he comes to the plate?
'Everybody acts like they hate him, but what do they do when the Dodgers don't let him hit?'
'Ten years from now, guaranteed, everyone out here will be telling their kids that they saw the great Barry Bonds play,' says Chavez.
And, boy, did he 'suck.'

An Accenture publication called 'Centerpoint' just interviewed me, as a new member of the research labs.

The really interesting machine, the one we're all pretending is just around the corner, is basically a domestic contraption the size of a bad armoire—something with cables like ivy, impossible to move without bribing friends, and guaranteed to annoy whoever has to dust around it—and it has not yet been invented.
But it's going to be great.
Or anyway great in the way elevators or radiators are great: transformative, slightly ugly, full of practical grievance.
How do you explain your job to your family?
I tell them that I'm an inventor.
Which sounds grandiose until you specify the scale, because mostly I invent phrases, interactions, little conceptual tools—ways for ordinary people to encounter systems without needing a priesthood.
A lot of invention is just deciding how a thing greets you, what it calls itself, what kind of patience it assumes on your part; an interface is office signage with delusions of grandeur.
You can patent a widget if you like, but the real work is often social choreography—habits, thresholds, permissions, the tiny rituals by which a machine gets invited into a room.
For example, the message 'Abort, retry, fail'.
That's a marvelous little fossil: three machine imperatives in a trench coat, a panicked stage manager barking orders at a user who hasn't been told what play they're in.
It tells you a whole era's theory of authority, because screens don't merely report states of affairs—they teach people whether they are being blamed, instructed, or welcomed.
Besides your cell phone, which gadget do you use the most?
Who has the time?
I like a meerschaum pipe, a German car, a good kitchen knife, or a ballpoint pen.
Those are technologies too, and in some ways better behaved ones: they do not ring in your pocket demanding a moral accounting of your whereabouts.
I might get a cellphone in ten years.
Selective technophilia is underrated; constant availability is not obviously the summit of civilization.
What was the first electronic device you took apart to see how it worked?
Did you get it back together again?
It was something with a little gearbox inside, full of white plastic gearlings.
And no, those things never, ever go back together again.
It's pure entropy.
Describe (as tastefully as possible) your fantasy convergence device.
I think that the things that make _people_ converge, in physical spaces, are the most important technologies.
So the literal answer would be some miraculous pocket object, a universal remote for culture, but that's too small a fantasy.

What I actually want is an architectural-social system, part town square, part switchboard, part public bench, part instant-message window with better shoes—something that gets bodies into rooms, gives them legibility, timing, chairs if necessary, and a reason to attend to the same thing at once.
Television, the web, and online gaming are not that system, though they suggest elements of it.
IM may point a way forward.

The problem isn't merely transmission but assembly: who shows up, how they know when, what they can do once they're there, and how a medium acknowledges that collective presence without flattening it.
We're trying to put a book's worth of information all on one screen, sort of like a really smart piece of microfiche.
What piece of advice would you give to the young people of today?
I had a physics professor who met Einstein once, as a young student at Oxford.
So I'll just relate what he said to me.
'We met Einstein in a hallway.
They asked us if we had any questions for Herr Doktor Einstein, and we didn't know what to say.
So they asked Einstein if he had anything to say to the students.
He said, 'Never believe anything that you read in the newspapers.''
